sourceRefs.exactPassage: **A DNA assay describes sequence and copy evidence in its tested material. Coverage and confidence come before the treatment story.**

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Variant calling assesses whether observed sequence or regional evidence supports a difference from a reference or comparison sample. Evidence quality, independent fragments, local depth, error models and the alteration class matter. Annotation describes possible consequence after calling; neither annotation nor a passed filter independently proves function or treatment relevance. Negative calls retain the workflow coverage and detection limits.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:variant-calling: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Sequencing infers base order from prepared material. Panels target selected regions; exomes primarily target exons; genomes cover coding and noncoding territory broadly. None guarantees uniform usable local evidence or analysis of every alteration class. Read length, territory, molecule independence, quality and validated use are separate features. Methylation requires an appropriate preparation and analysis rather than a sequencing category name.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Calling uses existing reads, a reference assembly and optional comparison files; a new confirmation assay can consume more material. Report coordinates, alleles, support, quality, filters and defined fractions/copy estimates. Retain caller version, detectable regions/classes and thresholds. Contamination, damage, misalignment and reference mismatch require specimen-specific end-to-end validation; filter thresholds are not treatment thresholds.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:variant-calling: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Paired tumour and an appropriate nonmalignant comparator help attribute a finding. Jones and colleagues' 2015 paired analyses showed why tumour-only interpretation can misclassify inherited findings. The normal comparator also needs adequate evidence at the site. In a fictional repair-gene example, 32 alternate reads among 160 usable reads give a 20 per cent observed fraction; an adequate matched normal lacking the change supports somatic origin in those sampled tissues. Neither that attribution nor a second adequate confirmation establishes that the change drives the cancer, disrupts repair or predicts treatment response. A familiar gene and a credible sequence call answer different questions from measured RNA, protein function and clinical actionability.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A confirmation should test the suspected weakness. Check specimen identity and tissue, preparation, alteration class, usable local coverage, read quality and alignment; a high average depth does not establish adequate evidence at the disputed site. Reformatting one call or rerunning the same reads does not create independent molecular evidence. A separate preparation or a method with different relevant failure modes may help; a different brand name alone does not establish independence. In a fictional comparison, assay A reports a low-fraction variant and B reports none without site coverage. B has not disproved A. Request the exact site, usable local support, class-specific detection limit, specimen and time point. If both tests were adequate, reconcile the discrepancy, including sampling different populations or times, before building further interpretations.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: [Hereditary breast-cancer genes](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/hereditary-risk/hereditary-breast-cancer-genes) explains why a familiar gene name does not establish inherited risk. [Germline testing](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/hereditary-risk/germline-testing) adds the distinction between a pathogenic result, an uncertain variant and an informative or uninformative negative. Tumor-only inference cannot replace that interpretation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Germline testing examines DNA from an appropriate non-tumour specimen, often blood or saliva, for constitutional variants. Many are inherited; a constitutional change can also arise newly. Tumour sequencing can reveal a finding that needs germline confirmation, but it does not establish its origin. A multigene panel and a targeted test for a known family variant answer different questions.

Testing includes consent, review of personal and family history, specimen collection, laboratory analysis and interpretation. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic finding may inform care and testing of relatives. It does not guarantee that cancer will occur or that a particular treatment will work. A variant of uncertain significance is not a pathogenic result and should not direct clinical management. A negative result must be interpreted against the genes and variant types the assay could detect and whether a causative family variant is already known.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:germline-testing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider two fictional negative reports. In one family, a harmful BRCA1 variant is already known and a suitable assay excludes that specific variant in the person tested. This is a true negative for that family finding, not a guarantee against all cancer. In another family, several relatives have had cancer but no causative family variant is known and a panel finds none. That result can be uninformative: family history can remain relevant without proving that a hidden mutation exists. A larger panel can add uncertain findings rather than a clearer explanation. Cascade testing means testing relatives for a confirmed family finding with their own consent and interpretation.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:germline-testing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Detection and interpretation are separate. The laboratory searches the regions and types of changes its method covers, then classifies a detected variant using evidence such as population frequency, segregation within families and functional studies. The ACMG/AMP framework uses pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign and benign categories; classifications can change as evidence develops. A VUS does not measure how severe an existing cancer is. That framework concerns Mendelian variant interpretation, not a complete rule for somatic drug selection.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: A fictional tumor has a splice-site change in repair gene R and loss of the other parental region. [Copy number and loss of heterozygosity (LOH)](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/sequencing-basics/copy-number-and-loh) separate the total count from which parental contributions remain. Its normal comparison does not show the variant within the assay's scope. A copy-aware model estimates that the retained cancer-cell copies carry it.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Biallelic inactivation concerns whether either parental contribution still supplies useful function in the relevant cancer-cell population, rather than simply counting two physical DNA copies or two events somewhere in a tissue. A damaging change plus loss of the other contribution can support it, but phasing, allele-specific copy state, consequence and cell mixture matter. High VAF alone cannot establish this state. Nguyen and colleagues' pan-cancer analysis associated particular biallelic repair-gene alterations with genomic damage patterns; that association does not make every variant in every repair gene functionally equivalent or establish present drug sensitivity.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: [Human leukocyte antigen loss of heterozygosity (HLA-LOH)](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/sequencing-basics/hla-loh) is a locus-specific copy question. Genomic allele loss, surface expression and peptide presentation remain different readouts.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:hla: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:hla: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

- Replacing a clinical hereditary test with tumor-only inference.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Germline testing examines DNA from an appropriate non-tumour specimen, often blood or saliva, for constitutional variants. Many are inherited; a constitutional change can also arise newly. Tumour sequencing can reveal a finding that needs germline confirmation, but it does not establish its origin. A multigene panel and a targeted test for a known family variant answer different questions.

Testing includes consent, review of personal and family history, specimen collection, laboratory analysis and interpretation. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic finding may inform care and testing of relatives. It does not guarantee that cancer will occur or that a particular treatment will work. A variant of uncertain significance is not a pathogenic result and should not direct clinical management. A negative result must be interpreted against the genes and variant types the assay could detect and whether a causative family variant is already known.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:germline-testing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider two fictional negative reports. In one family, a harmful BRCA1 variant is already known and a suitable assay excludes that specific variant in the person tested. This is a true negative for that family finding, not a guarantee against all cancer. In another family, several relatives have had cancer but no causative family variant is known and a panel finds none. That result can be uninformative: family history can remain relevant without proving that a hidden mutation exists. A larger panel can add uncertain findings rather than a clearer explanation. Cascade testing means testing relatives for a confirmed family finding with their own consent and interpretation.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:germline-testing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Detection and interpretation are separate. The laboratory searches the regions and types of changes its method covers, then classifies a detected variant using evidence such as population frequency, segregation within families and functional studies. The ACMG/AMP framework uses pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign and benign categories; classifications can change as evidence develops. A VUS does not measure how severe an existing cancer is. That framework concerns Mendelian variant interpretation, not a complete rule for somatic drug selection.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Variant calling assesses whether observed sequence or regional evidence supports a difference from a reference or comparison sample. Evidence quality, independent fragments, local depth, error models and the alteration class matter. Annotation describes possible consequence after calling; neither annotation nor a passed filter independently proves function or treatment relevance. Negative calls retain the workflow coverage and detection limits.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Sequencing infers base order from prepared material. Panels target selected regions; exomes primarily target exons; genomes cover coding and noncoding territory broadly. None guarantees uniform usable local evidence or analysis of every alteration class. Read length, territory, molecule independence, quality and validated use are separate features. Methylation requires an appropriate preparation and analysis rather than a sequencing category name.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna-splicing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A junction read supports a local RNA join, not necessarily a complete isoform. Gene-level counts can hide transcript differences. RNA quality, read coverage, reference version and cell mixture affect interpretation; protein quantity and function need separate evidence.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna-splicing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional repair-gene example, a high gene-level RNA count can include abnormal splice products and messages from normal neighbours. A reproducible abnormal junction supports a local RNA join, rather than a complete transcript, its protein or its originating DNA allele. An intronic DNA base may be removed during processing, so a mature-junction read need not contain that base. Assigning the product to a particular allele needs suitable linking sequence or another justified allele-specific measurement, with cell-source and reference checks. RNA directly examines the processing product; the gene-level count cannot settle the protein-function question.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Perou and colleagues profiled 65 surgical specimens from 42 patients on cDNA microarrays of 8,102 genes and found the tumours could be classified into subtypes distinguished by pervasive differences in gene expression, the origin of the intrinsic subtypes luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like and normal-like (Perou 2000). The Cancer Genome Atlas integrated copy number, methylation, exome, mRNA, microRNA and protein data across primary breast cancers, confirmed four main classes, found TP53, PIK3CA and GATA3 the only genes mutated in more than 10 percent overall, and showed basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, implying a related aetiology and similar therapeutic opportunities (TCGA 2012). Triple-negative and basal-like overlap but are not identical: of 412 triple-negative tumours 21.4 percent were non-basal-like, and of 473 basal-like tumours 31.5 percent were not triple-negative; triple-negative tumours classified as luminal or HER2-enriched had expression profiles indistinguishable from their non-triple-negative counterparts, most HER2-enriched triple-negative tumours lacked HER2 amplification, and the authors suggest triple-negative trials stratify by basal-like versus non-basal-like expression (Prat 2013). In the population-based Carolina Breast Cancer Study, using immunohistochemical surrogates (ER, PR and HER2 negative with cytokeratin 5/6 or HER1 positive), basal-like tumours were found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 14 percent of postmenopausal African American and 16 percent of non-African American women; they had more TP53 mutations (44 against 15 percent), higher mitotic index and grade, and among the shortest breast cancer-specific survival (Carey 2006). Basal-like cancers are the typical cancer of BRCA1 carriers, and adenoid cystic carcinoma is a special type of basal-like tumour with an excellent outlook (Ghabach 2010), a reminder that an expression label does not establish a uniform behaviour or exact cell ancestry. PAM50 basal-like and Lehmann BL1/BL2 belong to different classifiers; a PAM50 basal-like call does not by itself assign either Lehmann profile.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

An integrity score is therefore not a universal pass or fail rule for every RNA assay; input, preparation and intended measurement still matter.

This is evidence of recovery under that protocol, not equivalence of all fresh, snap-frozen and viable-cryopreserved samples or a guaranteed turnaround. The handling history, recovery, malignant identity and assay quality need checking for the intended experiment. Preserved molecular material alone does not establish a recoverable living model. coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: RNA carries cellular messages; bulk sequencing samples those messages from combined tissue after protocol-specific capture and preparation. Analysis assigns usable observations to genes or transcripts and applies a defined comparison scale. A change can reflect cell composition, expression within cells or both. Gene totals can conceal transcript differences, and pooled RNA does not directly establish protein localisation, pathway flux or drug dependence.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Before comparing profiles, check for [batch effects](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/transcriptomics/batch-effects): systematic differences associated with preparation or analysis. If all baseline samples use one method and all follow-up samples another, their contributions cannot be separated from that comparison alone. Normalizing counts does not supply the missing comparison. [Counts and normalization](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/transcriptomics/counts-normalization) explain what changing the denominator can and cannot resolve.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Perou and colleagues profiled 65 surgical specimens from 42 patients on cDNA microarrays of 8,102 genes and found the tumours could be classified into subtypes distinguished by pervasive differences in gene expression, the origin of the intrinsic subtypes luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like and normal-like (Perou 2000). The Cancer Genome Atlas integrated copy number, methylation, exome, mRNA, microRNA and protein data across primary breast cancers, confirmed four main classes, found TP53, PIK3CA and GATA3 the only genes mutated in more than 10 percent overall, and showed basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, implying a related aetiology and similar therapeutic opportunities (TCGA 2012). Triple-negative and basal-like overlap but are not identical: of 412 triple-negative tumours 21.4 percent were non-basal-like, and of 473 basal-like tumours 31.5 percent were not triple-negative; triple-negative tumours classified as luminal or HER2-enriched had expression profiles indistinguishable from their non-triple-negative counterparts, most HER2-enriched triple-negative tumours lacked HER2 amplification, and the authors suggest triple-negative trials stratify by basal-like versus non-basal-like expression (Prat 2013). In the population-based Carolina Breast Cancer Study, using immunohistochemical surrogates (ER, PR and HER2 negative with cytokeratin 5/6 or HER1 positive), basal-like tumours were found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 14 percent of postmenopausal African American and 16 percent of non-African American women; they had more TP53 mutations (44 against 15 percent), higher mitotic index and grade, and among the shortest breast cancer-specific survival (Carey 2006). Basal-like cancers are the typical cancer of BRCA1 carriers, and adenoid cystic carcinoma is a special type of basal-like tumour with an excellent outlook (Ghabach 2010), a reminder that an expression label does not establish a uniform behaviour or exact cell ancestry. PAM50 basal-like and Lehmann BL1/BL2 belong to different classifiers; a PAM50 basal-like call does not by itself assign either Lehmann profile.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A junction read supports a local RNA join, not necessarily a complete isoform. Gene-level counts can hide transcript differences. RNA quality, read coverage, reference version and cell mixture affect interpretation; protein quantity and function need separate evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional repair-gene example, a high gene-level RNA count can include abnormal splice products and messages from normal neighbours. A reproducible abnormal junction supports a local RNA join, rather than a complete transcript, its protein or its originating DNA allele. An intronic DNA base may be removed during processing, so a mature-junction read need not contain that base. Assigning the product to a particular allele needs suitable linking sequence or another justified allele-specific measurement, with cell-source and reference checks. RNA directly examines the processing product; the gene-level count cannot settle the protein-function question.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Mass-spectrometry and antibody-based methods measure different protein-derived signals under defined workflows. A primary yeast study measured protein expression alongside phosphorylation and showed why a changed phosphopeptide signal can reflect protein abundance as well as phosphorylation. That methodological result is not a validated cancer-treatment rule. Targeted plasma-protein assays likewise require evidence about recovery, calibration and quantitative range. A protein measurement, modification-site signal, functional pathway dependence and prediction of treatment benefit are distinct claims. Beausoleil and colleagues introduced the Ascore, a probability-based score for how likely a phosphorylation site is correctly localised from site-determining ions in tandem mass spectra, alongside a target-decoy measure of dataset error (2006). In yeast, 25 per cent of seemingly differential phosphopeptides were attributable to changes in protein expression once phosphopeptide ratios were calibrated by protein levels (Wu and colleagues, 2011). In human ovarian tumour and breast cancer xenograft tissue collected without vascular interruption, rapid phosphorylation changes were seen in up to 24 per cent of the phosphoproteome after defined ischaemic intervals, while the global proteome and most of more than 25,000 quantified phosphosites were unchanged after 60 minutes; phosphopeptides in that study were enriched by immobilised metal (Fe3+) affinity chromatography before analysis (Mertins and colleagues, 2014).
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:proteomics: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference). Kinases add phosphate and phosphatases remove it, as the existing phosphorylation record states, and a larger phosphopeptide signal is not a universal sign of greater activity. Enrichment changes what is recovered, so a phosphopeptide sample is not an unbiased count of all proteins. Site localisation is separate from peptide identification and carries its own confidence. A phosphopeptide intensity reflects the source-protein amount, the modified fraction and recovery, so intensity or fold change is not occupancy. A set of supported sites can inform a pathway hypothesis; it does not measure the pathway's rate, prove dependence or show benefit from a drug, and a kinase inferred from a pattern is not measured causality.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:proteomics: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference built on the ICH definitions). A signal detected below the quantification limit is meaningful as detection, but it does not support a reliable amount, and neither it nor non-detection means biological zero. An upper limit also bounds the range, and a saturated response cannot separate larger inputs. Keep the denominator with every amount (for example femtomoles per microgram of total extracted protein or a concentration per volume), because it describes the mixture and not receptors per malignant cell; a selected peptide is a proxy for its source protein and cannot count intact receptors or surface copies. Tight repeats show precision, which can coexist with systematic bias. A standard added after digestion can control later measurement but cannot correct material already lost.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:targeted-proteomics-quantification: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Bulk receptor abundance and staining mainly on blood vessels can both be correct: one measures a mixture and the other locates signal. Neither establishes target accessibility or treatment benefit. Staining also does not establish protein activity or cancer-cell dependence on that protein.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A useful IHC result identifies the block, fixation and section, antibody clone, retrieval and detection system, eligible cells and scored compartment. Cutting and staining use finite tissue. Report the percentage, intensity, location and named scoring scale, together with expected-positive tissue, relevant internal controls and background assessment. Poor preservation, nonspecific binding, few eligible cells, heterogeneous staining and observer variation can limit interpretation. Validation must fit the assay and its intended use; a research measurement is not automatically a clinical selection test.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A controlled perturbation deliberately changes a defined factor and measures the response against appropriate comparison conditions. Vehicle, positive, negative and mechanism controls answer different questions. A reproducible response can support an experimental claim without establishing its proposed mechanism or patient benefit. Baseline growth, timing, dose and the actual unit assigned to treatment matter.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:controlled-perturbation: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Mass-spectrometry and antibody-based methods measure different protein-derived signals under defined workflows. A primary yeast study measured protein expression alongside phosphorylation and showed why a changed phosphopeptide signal can reflect protein abundance as well as phosphorylation. That methodological result is not a validated cancer-treatment rule. Targeted plasma-protein assays likewise require evidence about recovery, calibration and quantitative range. A protein measurement, modification-site signal, functional pathway dependence and prediction of treatment benefit are distinct claims. Beausoleil and colleagues introduced the Ascore, a probability-based score for how likely a phosphorylation site is correctly localised from site-determining ions in tandem mass spectra, alongside a target-decoy measure of dataset error (2006). In yeast, 25 per cent of seemingly differential phosphopeptides were attributable to changes in protein expression once phosphopeptide ratios were calibrated by protein levels (Wu and colleagues, 2011). In human ovarian tumour and breast cancer xenograft tissue collected without vascular interruption, rapid phosphorylation changes were seen in up to 24 per cent of the phosphoproteome after defined ischaemic intervals, while the global proteome and most of more than 25,000 quantified phosphosites were unchanged after 60 minutes; phosphopeptides in that study were enriched by immobilised metal (Fe3+) affinity chromatography before analysis (Mertins and colleagues, 2014).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference). Kinases add phosphate and phosphatases remove it, as the existing phosphorylation record states, and a larger phosphopeptide signal is not a universal sign of greater activity. Enrichment changes what is recovered, so a phosphopeptide sample is not an unbiased count of all proteins. Site localisation is separate from peptide identification and carries its own confidence. A phosphopeptide intensity reflects the source-protein amount, the modified fraction and recovery, so intensity or fold change is not occupancy. A set of supported sites can inform a pathway hypothesis; it does not measure the pathway's rate, prove dependence or show benefit from a drug, and a kinase inferred from a pattern is not measured causality.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference built on the ICH definitions). A signal detected below the quantification limit is meaningful as detection, but it does not support a reliable amount, and neither it nor non-detection means biological zero. An upper limit also bounds the range, and a saturated response cannot separate larger inputs. Keep the denominator with every amount (for example femtomoles per microgram of total extracted protein or a concentration per volume), because it describes the mixture and not receptors per malignant cell; a selected peptide is a proxy for its source protein and cannot count intact receptors or surface copies. Tight repeats show precision, which can coexist with systematic bias. A standard added after digestion can control later measurement but cannot correct material already lost.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A useful IHC result identifies the block, fixation and section, antibody clone, retrieval and detection system, eligible cells and scored compartment. Cutting and staining use finite tissue. Report the percentage, intensity, location and named scoring scale, together with expected-positive tissue, relevant internal controls and background assessment. Poor preservation, nonspecific binding, few eligible cells, heterogeneous staining and observer variation can limit interpretation. Validation must fit the assay and its intended use; a research measurement is not automatically a clinical selection test.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A controlled perturbation deliberately changes a defined factor and measures the response against appropriate comparison conditions. coverageEvidence.excerpt: A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Protein kinases commonly transfer phosphate from ATP to a substrate, producing ADP. Protein phosphatases remove phosphate by hydrolysis without regenerating ATP. A modification can affect catalysis, binding, localization or interactions; sites on one protein can have different functions. Src experiments demonstrated an inhibitory tail-phosphorylation mechanism in their defined preparation, so phosphorylation should not be treated as universal activation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Mass-spectrometry and antibody-based methods measure different protein-derived signals under defined workflows. A primary yeast study measured protein expression alongside phosphorylation and showed why a changed phosphopeptide signal can reflect protein abundance as well as phosphorylation. That methodological result is not a validated cancer-treatment rule. Targeted plasma-protein assays likewise require evidence about recovery, calibration and quantitative range. A protein measurement, modification-site signal, functional pathway dependence and prediction of treatment benefit are distinct claims. Beausoleil and colleagues introduced the Ascore, a probability-based score for how likely a phosphorylation site is correctly localised from site-determining ions in tandem mass spectra, alongside a target-decoy measure of dataset error (2006). In yeast, 25 per cent of seemingly differential phosphopeptides were attributable to changes in protein expression once phosphopeptide ratios were calibrated by protein levels (Wu and colleagues, 2011). In human ovarian tumour and breast cancer xenograft tissue collected without vascular interruption, rapid phosphorylation changes were seen in up to 24 per cent of the phosphoproteome after defined ischaemic intervals, while the global proteome and most of more than 25,000 quantified phosphosites were unchanged after 60 minutes; phosphopeptides in that study were enriched by immobilised metal (Fe3+) affinity chromatography before analysis (Mertins and colleagues, 2014).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A reverse-phase protein array places sample lysates on an array and measures selected proteins or modifications with antibodies. The original tissue study examined signaling proteins in defined cell populations. A later study used phosphatase treatment as an independent control when characterizing phospho-antibodies for frozen and fixed tissue. Signal specificity, input preparation and validation matter. A lysate measurement does not restore the spatial arrangement lost during extraction, and phosphorylation signal needs interpretation alongside protein abundance. In the original reverse-phase protein microarray, the whole repertoire of a patient's tissue proteins from laser-capture microdissected cell populations is immobilised and probed, in contrast to earlier arrays that immobilise the probe, and precision and linearity were tested with microarrayed dilution curves of a standard protein and loading was normalised with an actin control (Paweletz and colleagues, 2001). Because target detection relies on a single antibody, RNA interference was used to test antibody performance: two anti-EGFR antibodies detected knockdown at different rates, and four of ten anti-STAT3 antibodies detected STAT3 knockdown at 80 to 85 per cent (Mannsperger and colleagues, 2010). Ischaemia changed phosphorylation in human ovarian tumour tissue and breast cancer xenografts, which supports recording how tissue was collected and preserved without setting a universal safe delay (Mertins and colleagues, 2014).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A primary multilaboratory study evaluated isotope-dilution multiple-reaction-monitoring assays for selected plasma proteins, examining recovery, reproducibility, linear range, detection and quantification limits. The performance belonged to the tested materials, analytes and protocols. It was not a universal certificate for all proteins or specimens. A reported protein amount should retain its measured peptide, calibration approach, sample preparation and supported range. An NIH workshop report on targeted mass spectrometry found no consensus on the criteria for a successful peptide assay and set out three tiers of assay performance, with response and calibration curves generated for each analyte in the relevant matrix to establish limits of detection and quantification; quantification rests on precursor-product ion pairs, called transitions, shown to be free of interference, and a surrogate protein standard must be shown to behave like the native analyte in tests of recovery after adding a known amount (Carr and colleagues, 2014). Stable-isotope-labelled internal standard peptides with the sequence of the analyte are spiked into the digest, and extended peptides or recombinant proteins can compensate for variability in digestion (Hoofnagle and colleagues, 2016). A multilaboratory plasma study reported reproducibility, recovery, linear range and limits of detection and quantification at microgram-per-millilitre protein concentrations (Addona and colleagues, 2009).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference built on the ICH definitions). A signal detected below the quantification limit is meaningful as detection, but it does not support a reliable amount, and neither it nor non-detection means biological zero. An upper limit also bounds the range, and a saturated response cannot separate larger inputs. Keep the denominator with every amount (for example femtomoles per microgram of total extracted protein or a concentration per volume), because it describes the mixture and not receptors per malignant cell; a selected peptide is a proxy for its source protein and cannot count intact receptors or surface copies. Tight repeats show precision, which can coexist with systematic bias. A standard added after digestion can control later measurement but cannot correct material already lost.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The oestrogen receptor is an intracellular protein involved in responses to oestrogen and regulation of gene expression. A clinical ER result measures receptor staining in identified tumour-cell nuclei, not the amount of oestrogen in blood or every downstream signal.

The ASCO/CAP invasive-breast guideline uses validated immunohistochemistry: at least 1% stained tumour-cell nuclei is positive, below 1% is negative, and 1% to 10% is reported as ER-low positive. These cancers are heterogeneous and can have features resembling ER-negative disease, but they remain ER-positive. Limited evidence suggests possible endocrine benefit, so the category supports consideration of endocrine treatment rather than a guaranteed response or a treatment mandate.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The progesterone receptor is an intracellular hormone-response protein. Its tissue stain does not measure circulating progesterone or every interaction with ER signalling. In invasive breast cancer, the ASCO/CAP guideline uses at least 1% positive tumour-cell nuclei for PR positivity and below 1% for negativity; ER-low positive is an ER-specific reporting category.

HR-positive is commonly used for ER-positive, PR-positive or both. Preserve the individual results: ER-positive/PR-negative is not hormone-receptor-negative or triple-negative. PR is primarily prognostic within ER-positive invasive disease. An unusual ER-negative/PR-positive combination should prompt review of the ER stain and controls, not an automatic inference about eligibility for endocrine treatment or a CDK4/6 inhibitor.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
HER2-low generally denotes IHC 1+ or IHC 2+ with a negative ISH result in the relevant breast-cancer context. HER2-ultralow denotes the IHC 0 pattern with membrane staining used in DESTINY-Breast06 and the corresponding U.S. ENHERTU label. These are measured categories with assay and reporting context. The September 2026 CAP template records the membrane-staining pattern as negative score 0+, separately from negative score 0 with no detected membrane staining.

DESTINY-Breast04 studied previously chemotherapy-treated HER2-low metastatic disease, including hormone receptor-positive and hormone receptor-negative participants. DESTINY-Breast06 studied hormone receptor-positive disease after endocrine therapy without prior chemotherapy for metastatic disease; its primary comparison concerned HER2-low disease and its ultralow analysis was exploratory. Neither trial establishes that every low-expression category is one biological disease or validates a cutoff for every ADC. The U.S. ENHERTU HER2-low and HER2-ultralow breast indications require an FDA-authorized HER2 test and unresectable or metastatic disease. One use is HR-positive HER2-low or HER2-ultralow disease that has progressed on one or more endocrine therapies in the metastatic setting. A separate HER2-low use requires prior chemotherapy in the metastatic setting, or recurrence during or within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy. The latter low-expression use does not require HR-positive disease; the ultralow indication does. The score alone does not establish eligibility or individual benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
RAD51 nuclear foci are assemblies of a protein involved in homologous recombination. Their interpretation depends on the sampled tumour cells, cell-cycle state, damage, staining, scoring and controls. A low count without enough informative cycling cells is uninformative rather than proof that repair is absent. The assay is a functional surrogate, not direct observation of every completed repair event.

Cruz and colleagues in 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived breast cancer models and retrospective tumour specimens. Castroviejo-Bermejo and colleagues separately compared RAD51 and genomic HRD scores against olaparib response in breast cancer xenografts, then assessed feasibility in archival breast samples, including PALB2-related cancers. The latter clinical samples established feasibility, rather than a randomised benefit from choosing treatment with the assay.

A scar records accumulated genomic changes; a suitably controlled RAD51 result asks about a present repair-related state. Repair-restoring changes and acquired foci were observed in selected resistant BRCA-mutated breast cancers, but those small cohorts do not establish a universal treatment-switch rule. Use the actual assay version, informative-cell requirements and intended-use validation. A research score cannot replace the biomarker, disease and companion-test conditions of a medicine's label.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An epitope is a molecular feature recognised by an immune receptor; its definition depends on the receptor and the tested molecular preparation. Trastuzumab and pertuzumab both bind HER2 but at different epitopes, which is why they can be given together, and zanidatamab is a single antibody built to grab both spots at once. For T cells, the epitope is a short peptide fragment held in an HLA molecule on the cell surface; an alteration that changes recognition can permit escape, but its effects on processing, display and other cell functions need their own evidence. The epitope an antibody recognises can be a continuous stretch of sequence or a surface formed by folding, so distant parts of the chain can meet; accessibility matters, and binding to an isolated protein does not show the same site is reachable on an intact cell. For a conventional T-cell receptor the target is the peptide together with the restricting HLA molecule, and the same peptide on another HLA molecule is a different recognition surface.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

points.heading: A second example: a delivery address
points.requirement: Carry every factual, numeric, causal and interpretive clause, or an explicit supported correction. Exact field containment alone cannot establish semantic acceptance.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: A surface receptor is abundant on cancer cells. A medicine may use it as an address to deliver a payload. The receptor need not be the growth driver for that delivery strategy to work. Conversely, a signaling inhibitor seeks a useful change in pathway behavior; surface abundance is not the same selection rule.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
HER2-low generally denotes IHC 1+ or IHC 2+ with a negative ISH result in the relevant breast-cancer context. HER2-ultralow denotes the IHC 0 pattern with membrane staining used in DESTINY-Breast06 and the corresponding U.S. ENHERTU label. These are measured categories with assay and reporting context. The September 2026 CAP template records the membrane-staining pattern as negative score 0+, separately from negative score 0 with no detected membrane staining.

DESTINY-Breast04 studied previously chemotherapy-treated HER2-low metastatic disease, including hormone receptor-positive and hormone receptor-negative participants. DESTINY-Breast06 studied hormone receptor-positive disease after endocrine therapy without prior chemotherapy for metastatic disease; its primary comparison concerned HER2-low disease and its ultralow analysis was exploratory. Neither trial establishes that every low-expression category is one biological disease or validates a cutoff for every ADC. The U.S. ENHERTU HER2-low and HER2-ultralow breast indications require an FDA-authorized HER2 test and unresectable or metastatic disease. One use is HR-positive HER2-low or HER2-ultralow disease that has progressed on one or more endocrine therapies in the metastatic setting. A separate HER2-low use requires prior chemotherapy in the metastatic setting, or recurrence during or within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy. The latter low-expression use does not require HR-positive disease; the ultralow indication does. The score alone does not establish eligibility or individual benefit.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: [[wiki/education/concepts/measurement/proteins-and-spatial/immunopeptidomics|Immunopeptidomics]] asks a different protein-related question: which peptides were recovered from human leukocyte antigen complexes? Presentation is closer to an immune-target question than total gene expression, but does not establish recognition by itself.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A primary melanoma study used mass spectrometry to identify HLA-associated peptides from native tumor tissue and then evaluated selected mutated peptides with immune assays. This is stronger evidence of natural presentation in the sampled material than a binding prediction alone. The analytical observation still has a defined specimen and workflow. It does not automatically establish the abundance of a ligand on every cancer cell, receptor recognition or a treatment effect. A published protocol isolates MHC-peptide complexes by immunoaffinity capture, dissociates the peptides by acid denaturation, fractionates them by HPLC and identifies them by nano-UPLC tandem mass spectrometry, from cell lines and tissues (Purcell and colleagues, 2019). Capture starts from mild-detergent solubilised lysates (Chong and colleagues, 2018; Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020 immunoprecipitated HLA from soluble lysates), so a lysate is not a surface-only survey, and in multi-allele samples a peptide was assigned to the best-scoring allele or alleles by computation (Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020). Identification depends on the analysis: a deep-learning model trained on more than 300,000 synthetic peptides improved HLA peptide identification up to 7-fold and indicated that 87 per cent of the proposed proteasomally spliced HLA peptides may be incorrect (Wilhelm and colleagues, 2021). A quantitative tissue study isolated peptide-HLA complexes from snap-frozen tissue and used formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded blocks only for histology (Science Translational Medicine, 2022).

No source read here establishes that formalin-fixed tissue is usable for an assay validated on cells or frozen tissue; the lesson's statement that one protocol proposed an adaptation could not be checked (publisher page unavailable), so that claim is withheld and compatibility must be shown for the named method.
