coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Integration card for combining molecular layers (a reading guide, not a score). Measures: relationships among named layers, not one universal multi-omic score. How: match evidence records, check quality and comparability, harmonise features, compare or model, then evaluate the stated question. Input and tissue cost: existing assay data and metadata; computation uses no extra tissue, but each original assay has its own specimen cost. Output and units: a comparison, factors, clusters or predictions, with the model version and underlying units. Thresholds: specific to the method and validated task, and none applies to every integration. Failure modes: sample swaps, cell-mixture changes, batch confounding, missing data and information leaking into evaluation. Cannot establish alone: causation, malignant-cell target location or better treatment outcomes. Validation tier: research integration gives neither its inputs nor its resulting model a clinical status.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: OlympiA, trial NCT02032823 sponsored by AstraZeneca, NRG Oncology and the Breast International Group and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, showed that a year of the PARP inhibitor olaparib after standard treatment improves survival in women with germline BRCA mutations and high-risk, HER2-negative early breast cancer, about eighty percent of whom had triple-negative disease. coverageEvidence.excerpt: The U.S. olaparib label effective July 2025 permits olaparib plus bevacizumab maintenance for adults with HRD-positive advanced epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer in complete or partial response to first-line platinum; the specified HRD definition includes a deleterious or suspected-deleterious BRCA alteration and/or genomic instability, with an approved companion test. coverageEvidence.excerpt: The U.S. Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments program sets laboratory-quality requirements for testing human specimens. CMS distinguishes analytical oversight under that program from clinical validity, which concerns what a result means for a clinical condition. A research-use label describes intended purpose; a laboratory-developed-test description concerns how and where a test is developed and used. FDA product authorization concerns a specified product and intended use. These descriptions can coexist and do not form one universal ladder of clinical usefulness or payment.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: FDA guidance on research-use-only in vitro diagnostic products concerns their intended use, labeling and distribution. The label alone is not a complete account of analytical performance or clinical usefulness, and its legal framework should not be generalized to every research model or dataset. sourceRefs.exactPassage: - **Decision:** Establish estrogen receptor (ER) status in invasive breast cancer tissue, for its recognized pathology and endocrine-treatment assessment context.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The oestrogen receptor is an intracellular protein involved in responses to oestrogen and regulation of gene expression. A clinical ER result measures receptor staining in identified tumour-cell nuclei, not the amount of oestrogen in blood or every downstream signal.

The ASCO/CAP invasive-breast guideline uses validated immunohistochemistry: at least 1% stained tumour-cell nuclei is positive, below 1% is negative, and 1% to 10% is reported as ER-low positive. These cancers are heterogeneous and can have features resembling ER-negative disease, but they remain ER-positive. Limited evidence suggests possible endocrine benefit, so the category supports consideration of endocrine treatment rather than a guaranteed response or a treatment mandate.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:er-status: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The measurement route is tissue, identification of invasive tumour cells, a validated nuclear stain, review of controls, percentage and intensity, then interpretation. Keep the specimen/block and collection context; IHC uses tissue sections. Percentage counts positive nuclei among the intended tumour cells, while intensity describes stain strength. Poor preservation, artefact or failed controls can prevent interpretation: uninterpretable does not mean negative. A bulk RNA result does not replace validated clinical IHC. ASCO/CAP recommends ER testing in DCIS to assess potential endocrine risk reduction, with PR optional there; invasive and in-situ contexts should be stated.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:er-status: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: For a fictional invasive tumour with adequate controls, ER staining in 4% of tumour-cell nuclei is ER-low positive. It is not 4% predicted treatment benefit and is not rounded down to ER-negative because an RNA classifier says basal-like. Preserve the stain denominator, intensity and category alongside that separate expression result. If controls fail, resolve the testing problem before assigning a negative category. ER and PR results remain separate observations.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: DNA, RNA and protein can strengthen a consequence chain because they inspect different objects. They remain linked biologically. They can also share specimen contamination, wrong cell assignments or the same assumed variant list.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Integration card for combining molecular layers (a reading guide, not a score). Measures: relationships among named layers, not one universal multi-omic score. How: match evidence records, check quality and comparability, harmonise features, compare or model, then evaluate the stated question. Input and tissue cost: existing assay data and metadata; computation uses no extra tissue, but each original assay has its own specimen cost. Output and units: a comparison, factors, clusters or predictions, with the model version and underlying units. Thresholds: specific to the method and validated task, and none applies to every integration. Failure modes: sample swaps, cell-mixture changes, batch confounding, missing data and information leaking into evaluation. Cannot establish alone: causation, malignant-cell target location or better treatment outcomes. Validation tier: research integration gives neither its inputs nor its resulting model a clinical status.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: If three reports merely repeat one variant call, they are not three raw confirmations. If an RNA junction was independently measured, that adds a new observation. Write which kind of agreement occurred rather than counting report titles.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: OlympiA, trial NCT02032823 sponsored by AstraZeneca, NRG Oncology and the Breast International Group and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, showed that a year of the PARP inhibitor olaparib after standard treatment improves survival in women with germline BRCA mutations and high-risk, HER2-negative early breast cancer, about eighty percent of whom had triple-negative disease. It randomised 1,836 patients to olaparib or placebo, met its primary invasive disease-free survival endpoint and showed an overall survival benefit that was sustained at six years. It makes germline testing a treatment decision for every such patient, and whether the benefit extends to somatic or non-BRCA HRD alterations is the open question.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:olympia: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The U.S. olaparib label effective July 2025 permits olaparib plus bevacizumab maintenance for adults with HRD-positive advanced epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer in complete or partial response to first-line platinum; the specified HRD definition includes a deleterious or suspected-deleterious BRCA alteration and/or genomic instability, with an approved companion test. Its early-breast indication instead requires a deleterious or suspected-deleterious germline BRCA alteration, HER2-negative high-risk disease and prior neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy, with the approved test. A tumour-only BRCA finding or an arbitrary high scar number does not substitute for these conditions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. Eligibility exclusions, absent tumour, laboratory failures, missing outcomes and people not receiving the treatment belong to different steps. State whether the unit is a person, specimen or treatment comparison; one person can contribute more than one. A percentage among compared cases cannot describe everyone originally offered testing, and an analysis exclusion is not automatically a failed culture. Keep the drug, cancer, treatment history, outcome, clock and assay version attached rather than ranking different studies as competing accuracy scores.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:functional-drug-testing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The category concerns a device and a corresponding treatment use. FDA describes roles involving likely benefit, serious-adverse-effect risk or specified treatment monitoring. Check both the treatment and diagnostic labeling, including specimen, disease, biomarker and decision rule. A molecular report listing a drug is not by itself a companion-diagnostic authorization. Similar gene names do not establish assay interchangeability, and a positive result does not promise a response.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:companion-diagnostic-term: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Three examples separate intended uses. Validated ER immunohistochemistry in invasive breast cancer, with appropriate tissue handling, tumour-nucleus scoring and controls, has a marker-specific pathology and endocrine-treatment assessment role; it does not validate a new RNA score as a substitute. coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Residual tumour here means cancer remaining in the sampled tissue after treatment. For residual-tumour research, first support malignant-cell identity, then ask which recovered states, target messages and immune profiles are present. A stress programme does not establish a genetic clone or explain survival. In Kim and colleagues' twenty-person triple-negative breast-cancer study, longitudinal exome data and single-cell DNA/RNA data in eight participants supported selection of pre-existing genotypes alongside expression reprogramming under the studied treatment. This is not a universal resistance mechanism. Compare the sampled region, time, preparation, recovery and analysis before attributing a difference to treatment; a missing cluster need not have been eliminated. In a separate fictional calculation, an input suspension truly containing 4 percent malignant nuclei gives an expectation of 240 among 6,000 retained profiles only if malignant and other nuclei have equal inclusion through recovery, capture and quality filtering. Tissue-area cellularity is a different denominator. The calculation is neither a yield forecast nor an adequacy cutoff.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A primary melanoma study used mass spectrometry to identify HLA-associated peptides from native tumor tissue and then evaluated selected mutated peptides with immune assays. This is stronger evidence of natural presentation in the sampled material than a binding prediction alone. The analytical observation still has a defined specimen and workflow. It does not automatically establish the abundance of a ligand on every cancer cell, receptor recognition or a treatment effect. A published protocol isolates MHC-peptide complexes by immunoaffinity capture, dissociates the peptides by acid denaturation, fractionates them by HPLC and identifies them by nano-UPLC tandem mass spectrometry, from cell lines and tissues (Purcell and colleagues, 2019). Capture starts from mild-detergent solubilised lysates (Chong and colleagues, 2018; Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020 immunoprecipitated HLA from soluble lysates), so a lysate is not a surface-only survey, and in multi-allele samples a peptide was assigned to the best-scoring allele or alleles by computation (Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020). Identification depends on the analysis: a deep-learning model trained on more than 300,000 synthetic peptides improved HLA peptide identification up to 7-fold and indicated that 87 per cent of the proposed proteasomally spliced HLA peptides may be incorrect (Wilhelm and colleagues, 2021). A quantitative tissue study isolated peptide-HLA complexes from snap-frozen tissue and used formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded blocks only for histology (Science Translational Medicine, 2022).

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. Simoni found bystander CD8 cells recognizing viral rather than cancer epitopes in human lung and colorectal tumours; the study’s CD39 associations are not a universal test of every cell’s target. A functional assay compares defined effectors and targets with recognition and target-survival controls. Neither presence, cytokine release nor one killing assay reproduces every access barrier or establishes clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Residual tumour here means cancer remaining in the sampled tissue after treatment. For residual-tumour research, first support malignant-cell identity, then ask which recovered states, target messages and immune profiles are present. A stress programme does not establish a genetic clone or explain survival. In Kim and colleagues' twenty-person triple-negative breast-cancer study, longitudinal exome data and single-cell DNA/RNA data in eight participants supported selection of pre-existing genotypes alongside expression reprogramming under the studied treatment. This is not a universal resistance mechanism. Compare the sampled region, time, preparation, recovery and analysis before attributing a difference to treatment; a missing cluster need not have been eliminated. In a separate fictional calculation, an input suspension truly containing 4 percent malignant nuclei gives an expectation of 240 among 6,000 retained profiles only if malignant and other nuclei have equal inclusion through recovery, capture and quality filtering. Tissue-area cellularity is a different denominator. The calculation is neither a yield forecast nor an adequacy cutoff.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

Report a gene-by-barcode table with its UMI/read/probe counting unit. Cell calling, low-quality and doublet criteria are chemistry/version-specific. coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A primary melanoma study used mass spectrometry to identify HLA-associated peptides from native tumor tissue and then evaluated selected mutated peptides with immune assays. This is stronger evidence of natural presentation in the sampled material than a binding prediction alone. The analytical observation still has a defined specimen and workflow. It does not automatically establish the abundance of a ligand on every cancer cell, receptor recognition or a treatment effect. A published protocol isolates MHC-peptide complexes by immunoaffinity capture, dissociates the peptides by acid denaturation, fractionates them by HPLC and identifies them by nano-UPLC tandem mass spectrometry, from cell lines and tissues (Purcell and colleagues, 2019). Capture starts from mild-detergent solubilised lysates (Chong and colleagues, 2018; Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020 immunoprecipitated HLA from soluble lysates), so a lysate is not a surface-only survey, and in multi-allele samples a peptide was assigned to the best-scoring allele or alleles by computation (Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020). Identification depends on the analysis: a deep-learning model trained on more than 300,000 synthetic peptides improved HLA peptide identification up to 7-fold and indicated that 87 per cent of the proposed proteasomally spliced HLA peptides may be incorrect (Wilhelm and colleagues, 2021). A quantitative tissue study isolated peptide-HLA complexes from snap-frozen tissue and used formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded blocks only for histology (Science Translational Medicine, 2022).

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Staining recognises an antibody-defined molecular feature, or epitope, rather than automatically proving a complete functioning protein. In an invented repair-gene example, weaker staining in identified cancer cells than in normal neighbours supports a cell-specific signal difference if the controls are adequate. The antibody may recognise a fragment or more than one protein form, so this does not give the amount of intact useful repair protein. The relevant form and current repair need suitable measurements of their own. One validated method can sometimes answer several questions, but measuring one property does not establish every other one.

Check coherent marker evidence and the method of assignment; a mixture of markers does not by itself establish a new cell type. Pooling the counts from a selected set of profiles is pseudobulk. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. Simoni found bystander CD8 cells recognizing viral rather than cancer epitopes in human lung and colorectal tumours; the study’s CD39 associations are not a universal test of every cell’s target. A functional assay compares defined effectors and targets with recognition and target-survival controls. Neither presence, cytokine release nor one killing assay reproduces every access barrier or establishes clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The original RNA Integrity Number method summarized electrophoretic features to standardize quality assessment. DV200 describes the proportion of RNA fragments longer than 200 nucleotides. Comparisons of fixed and frozen tissue found that fragment-distribution measures and functional amplification assays could be more informative for particular workflows. The NCI preanalytical-variables study likewise found method-dependent sensitivity to handling effects. An integrity score is therefore not a universal pass or fail rule for every RNA assay; input, preparation and intended measurement still matter.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Residual tumour here means cancer remaining in the sampled tissue after treatment. For residual-tumour research, first support malignant-cell identity, then ask which recovered states, target messages and immune profiles are present. A stress programme does not establish a genetic clone or explain survival. In Kim and colleagues' twenty-person triple-negative breast-cancer study, longitudinal exome data and single-cell DNA/RNA data in eight participants supported selection of pre-existing genotypes alongside expression reprogramming under the studied treatment. This is not a universal resistance mechanism. Compare the sampled region, time, preparation, recovery and analysis before attributing a difference to treatment; a missing cluster need not have been eliminated. In a separate fictional calculation, an input suspension truly containing 4 percent malignant nuclei gives an expectation of 240 among 6,000 retained profiles only if malignant and other nuclei have equal inclusion through recovery, capture and quality filtering. Tissue-area cellularity is a different denominator. The calculation is neither a yield forecast nor an adequacy cutoff.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:hla: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Staining recognises an antibody-defined molecular feature, or epitope, rather than automatically proving a complete functioning protein. In an invented repair-gene example, weaker staining in identified cancer cells than in normal neighbours supports a cell-specific signal difference if the controls are adequate. The antibody may recognise a fragment or more than one protein form, so this does not give the amount of intact useful repair protein. The relevant form and current repair need suitable measurements of their own. One validated method can sometimes answer several questions, but measuring one property does not establish every other one.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: **DNA, RNA and protein are different things to measure. A change in one layer starts a question about the next.**
**DNA, RNA and protein are different things to measure. A change in one layer starts a question about the next.**

coverageEvidence.excerpt: DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:dna-term: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: RNA abundance reflects production, processing and degradation. Short sequencing reads do not prove that a full-length intact message was captured. A noncoding RNA can function without becoming a protein, and reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant biological contexts. RNA amount does not determine a fixed protein amount or activity.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:gene: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:protein: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:central-dogma-information-flow: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.
