sourceRefs.exactPassage: The recipe analogy helps: DNA is the stored recipe, RNA a working copy and protein a tool or product made from the instructions. A cell is more than a kitchen, though. It controls which recipes are copied, which messages persist and which products are used.

The recipe analogy helps: DNA is the stored recipe, RNA a working copy and protein a tool or product made from the instructions. A cell is more than a kitchen, though. It controls which recipes are copied, which messages persist and which products are used.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:dna-term: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: RNA abundance reflects production, processing and degradation. Short sequencing reads do not prove that a full-length intact message was captured. A noncoding RNA can function without becoming a protein, and reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant biological contexts. RNA amount does not determine a fixed protein amount or activity.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:gene: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:protein: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:central-dogma-information-flow: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:dna-term: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: RNA abundance reflects production, processing and degradation. Short sequencing reads do not prove that a full-length intact message was captured. A noncoding RNA can function without becoming a protein, and reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant biological contexts. RNA amount does not determine a fixed protein amount or activity.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation reads a coding message in codons to make a polypeptide. This information-flow description does not require every RNA to become protein. A promoter recruits transcription machinery. Enhancers influence transcription through regulatory interactions that can span distant DNA positions. Transcription factors recognize sequence features and participate in regulation. Chromatin, RNA processing and turnover, translation, protein processing and degradation all influence the eventual product. A transcript’s frame and reference context matter when interpreting a sequence change.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:ihc: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Staining recognises an antibody-defined molecular feature, or epitope, rather than automatically proving a complete functioning protein. In an invented repair-gene example, weaker staining in identified cancer cells than in normal neighbours supports a cell-specific signal difference if the controls are adequate. The antibody may recognise a fragment or more than one protein form, so this does not give the amount of intact useful repair protein. The relevant form and current repair need suitable measurements of their own. One validated method can sometimes answer several questions, but measuring one property does not establish every other one.

A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:

For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. sourceRefs.exactPassage: **A tumor specimen is a piece of tissue, not a jar of pure cancer cells. Know the neighbors before interpreting its signal.**

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Epithelium forms linings, coverings and glands; an epithelial cell is not necessarily malignant. A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath an epithelium, distinct from each cell’s lipid membrane. Stroma includes supporting cells, extracellular matrix and vascular structures, rather than only collagen or fibroblasts. Immune cells and other nonmalignant cells can contribute to a tumor specimen. The relevant compartments depend on the tissue and disease.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:epithelium-and-stroma: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Bulk RNA or protein measurements combine contributions from sampled cells. A stronger signal can reflect more cells of one type, changed expression within cells, or both. Spatial review and suitable cell markers help test attribution; a mixed-tissue result should not automatically be assigned to cancer cells. Normal and cancer breast atlases provide defined examples of this cellular diversity.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:epithelium-and-stroma: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An epithelial marker helps identify a cell compartment; a positive lineage stain alone does not establish malignancy or invasion. Tissue architecture matters. For an epithelial carcinoma, assessing in-situ versus invasive disease includes microscopic review of the basement membrane and surrounding tissue. The SEER summary-stage manual retains site-specific exceptions; this boundary is not a universal staging rule for every cancer.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:epithelium-and-stroma: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Bulk RNA sequencing measures captured messages pooled across a specimen. Cancer, immune and supporting cells can contribute different amounts of RNA; a higher signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells, or both. Zero detected reads does not establish biological absence. Source: Conesa et al., 2016 methods review, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-0881-8.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:bulk-rna-seq: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: From a typical normal acinus lumen outward, distinguish luminal epithelial cells, living myoepithelial cells, extracellular basement membrane and surrounding stroma. Stroma includes connective tissue, fat, vessels and immune cells. A basement membrane is neither a cell layer nor the plasma membrane around one cell.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:terminal-duct-lobular-unit: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An epithelial marker or abundant epithelial RNA can come from normal epithelium. A sample richer in glands and poorer in stroma can change a bulk measurement without a change within either cell type. Imaging, tissue morphology and protein staining observe different scales; a normal-breast atlas is a reference, not a stand-alone cancer diagnosis.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:terminal-duct-lobular-unit: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

points.entailment: Normal epithelium, cancer, supporting/vessel/immune populations and unequal RNA contributions are separated. points.heading: Picture the breast duct from the inside out
points.requirement: Carry every factual, numeric, causal and interpretive clause, or an explicit supported correction. Exact field containment alone cannot establish semantic acceptance.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: In [breast anatomy](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/anatomy-and-histology/breast-anatomy), small milk-producing lobules and their terminal duct form a **terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU)**. A lumen is an inner space; luminal cells face it. [Myoepithelial cells and the basement membrane](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/anatomy-and-histology/myoepithelial-cells-and-basement-membrane) help define normal compartments. Surrounding stroma contains cells, vessels and [extracellular matrix](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/tumor-microenvironment/extracellular-matrix).

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The breast contains an interconnected duct-lobular epithelial system within connective and fatty tissue. A terminal duct with its associated acini forms a terminal duct lobular unit. Tissue compartments and their proportions matter when interpreting imaging, microscopy or bulk molecular measurements. Histological diagnosis, grade, receptor status and disease extent require their own evidence.

NCI DCEG describes the TDLU as the origin of most breast cancer precursors and cancers. The names ductal and lobular are diagnostic morphology, not proof of an exact ancestral cell. Characteristic loss of E-cadherin in invasive lobular carcinoma reduces cell adhesion; diffuse growth in unconnected lines can make a lesion harder to feel or detect on imaging. The SEER description concerns this growth pattern rather than a universal test result for every lobular tumour.

Male breasts have ducts and may have lobules, but far fewer than female breasts; NCI describes lobular cancer as rare in men. Breast tissue and mammographic density change over life. Greater density is associated with higher breast-cancer risk and can obscure cancers on a mammogram; increasing age and childbearing are associated with lower density, alongside other influences. Mammographic density, TDLU involution and histological diagnosis are different observations.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:terminal-duct-lobular-unit: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The terminal duct lobular unit contains a terminal duct and its associated acini. Acini make milk during lactation; ducts carry it towards the nipple. Lobules and larger lobes are different levels of organisation. Their size and abundance vary with physiology and life stage; an illustrative branch count is not a fixed anatomical count. A schematic grouping bracket is an annotation, not a tissue capsule or basement membrane. NCI DCEG describes TDLU involution with physiological ageing and completion of childbearing as reductions in acini per unit and total unit counts. This is an observational normal-tissue description, not a diagnostic rule for an individual.

Likewise, ductal and lobular diagnostic names do not prove the precise ancestral location, and anatomical luminal position does not assign a molecular luminal subtype. A milk-flow diagram is not a cancer-progression sequence.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: An analyst may try to enrich malignant cells or assign individual cells to groups. Those steps can help, but the resulting label needs evidence. Cell appearance, multiple markers, acquired DNA changes and copy patterns can support malignancy. One epithelial marker cannot distinguish normal lining cells from cancer.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Support a malignant-cell assignment with tissue context, a coherent marker panel, suitable normal references and quality checks, rather than one marker or cluster name. In five primary glioblastomas, Patel and colleagues profiled 430 cells and inferred broad chromosome alterations by averaging RNA expression along chromosomes against normal reference profiles. This was RNA-based inference, not a direct DNA copy count or a breast diagnostic rule. A flat inferred profile can miss a malignant cell lacking a detectable broad change; focal alterations and point mutations can also be missed. Matched DNA, pathology and spatial evidence can corroborate an assignment, but bulk DNA does not identify every RNA barcode. Mixed markers may reflect ambient RNA or doublets. In another fictional mixed sample, vimentin RNA could come from fibroblasts or a changed cancer-cell programme. Even cell-attributed expression of that marker alone does not establish invasion, resistance or ancestry. Keep uncertain assignments uncertain.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional comparison, gene R is high in cancer cells, low in fibroblasts and similarly high in normal luminal epithelial cells. The first contrast supports higher expression than fibroblasts, even if it passes a statistical threshold; it does not establish cancer selectivity. The normal epithelial comparison addresses that claim more closely, while leaving other organs, cell states and target accessibility untested. If that reference group is tiny, contaminated or prepared differently, preserve the unresolved comparison rather than declaring selectivity or exact equality. Normal epithelial cells can also contribute familiar lineage markers to a tumour specimen. An image-based tumour mask is an assignment that needs validation for its actual method and specimens, rather than automatic proof that every included cell is malignant.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The breast contains an interconnected duct-lobular epithelial system within connective and fatty tissue. A terminal duct with its associated acini forms a terminal duct lobular unit. Tissue compartments and their proportions matter when interpreting imaging, microscopy or bulk molecular measurements. Histological diagnosis, grade, receptor status and disease extent require their own evidence.

NCI DCEG describes the TDLU as the origin of most breast cancer precursors and cancers. The names ductal and lobular are diagnostic morphology, not proof of an exact ancestral cell. Characteristic loss of E-cadherin in invasive lobular carcinoma reduces cell adhesion; diffuse growth in unconnected lines can make a lesion harder to feel or detect on imaging. The SEER description concerns this growth pattern rather than a universal test result for every lobular tumour.

Male breasts have ducts and may have lobules, but far fewer than female breasts; NCI describes lobular cancer as rare in men. Breast tissue and mammographic density change over life. Greater density is associated with higher breast-cancer risk and can obscure cancers on a mammogram; increasing age and childbearing are associated with lower density, alongside other influences. Mammographic density, TDLU involution and histological diagnosis are different observations.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The terminal duct lobular unit contains a terminal duct and its associated acini. Acini make milk during lactation; ducts carry it towards the nipple. A schematic grouping bracket is an annotation, not a tissue capsule or basement membrane. NCI DCEG describes TDLU involution with physiological ageing and completion of childbearing as reductions in acini per unit and total unit counts. This is an observational normal-tissue description, not a diagnostic rule for an individual.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Support a malignant-cell assignment with tissue context, a coherent marker panel, suitable normal references and quality checks, rather than one marker or cluster name. In five primary glioblastomas, Patel and colleagues profiled 430 cells and inferred broad chromosome alterations by averaging RNA expression along chromosomes against normal reference profiles. This was RNA-based inference, not a direct DNA copy count or a breast diagnostic rule. A flat inferred profile can miss a malignant cell lacking a detectable broad change; focal alterations and point mutations can also be missed. Matched DNA, pathology and spatial evidence can corroborate an assignment, but bulk DNA does not identify every RNA barcode. Mixed markers may reflect ambient RNA or doublets. In another fictional mixed sample, vimentin RNA could come from fibroblasts or a changed cancer-cell programme. Even cell-attributed expression of that marker alone does not establish invasion, resistance or ancestry. Keep uncertain assignments uncertain.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Next look for a coherent tumor-associated pattern. One research approach averages expression across neighboring genes on chromosomes to **infer large-scale copy-number alterations**. A pattern consistent with the tumor's genomic changes can support an assignment when combined with cell-family evidence. This is an inference from RNA abundance, not a direct count of DNA copies. In a primary glioblastoma study, Patel and colleagues combined inferred chromosomal patterns with expression profiles to separate probable normal cells from malignant populations. It illustrates a method in that setting, rather than a breast-cancer diagnostic rule.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Perou and colleagues profiled 65 surgical specimens from 42 patients on cDNA microarrays of 8,102 genes and found the tumours could be classified into subtypes distinguished by pervasive differences in gene expression, the origin of the intrinsic subtypes luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like and normal-like (Perou 2000). The Cancer Genome Atlas integrated copy number, methylation, exome, mRNA, microRNA and protein data across primary breast cancers, confirmed four main classes, found TP53, PIK3CA and GATA3 the only genes mutated in more than 10 percent overall, and showed basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, implying a related aetiology and similar therapeutic opportunities (TCGA 2012). Triple-negative and basal-like overlap but are not identical: of 412 triple-negative tumours 21.4 percent were non-basal-like, and of 473 basal-like tumours 31.5 percent were not triple-negative; triple-negative tumours classified as luminal or HER2-enriched had expression profiles indistinguishable from their non-triple-negative counterparts, most HER2-enriched triple-negative tumours lacked HER2 amplification, and the authors suggest triple-negative trials stratify by basal-like versus non-basal-like expression (Prat 2013). In the population-based Carolina Breast Cancer Study, using immunohistochemical surrogates (ER, PR and HER2 negative with cytokeratin 5/6 or HER1 positive), basal-like tumours were found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 14 percent of postmenopausal African American and 16 percent of non-African American women; they had more TP53 mutations (44 against 15 percent), higher mitotic index and grade, and among the shortest breast cancer-specific survival (Carey 2006). Basal-like cancers are the typical cancer of BRCA1 carriers, and adenoid cystic carcinoma is a special type of basal-like tumour with an excellent outlook (Ghabach 2010), a reminder that an expression label does not establish a uniform behaviour or exact cell ancestry. PAM50 basal-like and Lehmann BL1/BL2 belong to different classifiers; a PAM50 basal-like call does not by itself assign either Lehmann profile.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Imagine high vimentin RNA in a mixed specimen. **Vimentin** is associated with mesenchymal features and is also expressed by supporting cells. [Epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT)](/wiki/education/concepts/biology-basics/cells/epithelial-mesenchymal-transition) is a context-dependent change in cell programs, not a diagnosis from one marker.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Support a malignant-cell assignment with tissue context, a coherent marker panel, suitable normal references and quality checks, rather than one marker or cluster name. In five primary glioblastomas, Patel and colleagues profiled 430 cells and inferred broad chromosome alterations by averaging RNA expression along chromosomes against normal reference profiles. This was RNA-based inference, not a direct DNA copy count or a breast diagnostic rule. A flat inferred profile can miss a malignant cell lacking a detectable broad change; focal alterations and point mutations can also be missed. Matched DNA, pathology and spatial evidence can corroborate an assignment, but bulk DNA does not identify every RNA barcode. Mixed markers may reflect ambient RNA or doublets. In another fictional mixed sample, vimentin RNA could come from fibroblasts or a changed cancer-cell programme. Even cell-attributed expression of that marker alone does not establish invasion, resistance or ancestry. Keep uncertain assignments uncertain.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Now imagine two cancer cells fall in the same RNA cluster. They may have similar activity but different acquired mutations. Conversely, cells from the same genetic clone can use different programs. Genetic ancestry and transcriptional similarity need separate evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Perou and colleagues profiled 65 surgical specimens from 42 patients on cDNA microarrays of 8,102 genes and found the tumours could be classified into subtypes distinguished by pervasive differences in gene expression, the origin of the intrinsic subtypes luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like and normal-like (Perou 2000). The Cancer Genome Atlas integrated copy number, methylation, exome, mRNA, microRNA and protein data across primary breast cancers, confirmed four main classes, found TP53, PIK3CA and GATA3 the only genes mutated in more than 10 percent overall, and showed basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, implying a related aetiology and similar therapeutic opportunities (TCGA 2012). Triple-negative and basal-like overlap but are not identical: of 412 triple-negative tumours 21.4 percent were non-basal-like, and of 473 basal-like tumours 31.5 percent were not triple-negative; triple-negative tumours classified as luminal or HER2-enriched had expression profiles indistinguishable from their non-triple-negative counterparts, most HER2-enriched triple-negative tumours lacked HER2 amplification, and the authors suggest triple-negative trials stratify by basal-like versus non-basal-like expression (Prat 2013). In the population-based Carolina Breast Cancer Study, using immunohistochemical surrogates (ER, PR and HER2 negative with cytokeratin 5/6 or HER1 positive), basal-like tumours were found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 14 percent of postmenopausal African American and 16 percent of non-African American women; they had more TP53 mutations (44 against 15 percent), higher mitotic index and grade, and among the shortest breast cancer-specific survival (Carey 2006). Basal-like cancers are the typical cancer of BRCA1 carriers, and adenoid cystic carcinoma is a special type of basal-like tumour with an excellent outlook (Ghabach 2010), a reminder that an expression label does not establish a uniform behaviour or exact cell ancestry. PAM50 basal-like and Lehmann BL1/BL2 belong to different classifiers; a PAM50 basal-like call does not by itself assign either Lehmann profile.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Support a malignant-cell assignment with tissue context, a coherent marker panel, suitable normal references and quality checks, rather than one marker or cluster name. In five primary glioblastomas, Patel and colleagues profiled 430 cells and inferred broad chromosome alterations by averaging RNA expression along chromosomes against normal reference profiles. This was RNA-based inference, not a direct DNA copy count or a breast diagnostic rule. A flat inferred profile can miss a malignant cell lacking a detectable broad change; focal alterations and point mutations can also be missed. Matched DNA, pathology and spatial evidence can corroborate an assignment, but bulk DNA does not identify every RNA barcode. Mixed markers may reflect ambient RNA or doublets. In another fictional mixed sample, vimentin RNA could come from fibroblasts or a changed cancer-cell programme. Even cell-attributed expression of that marker alone does not establish invasion, resistance or ancestry. Keep uncertain assignments uncertain.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: RNA is distributed across cellular compartments. Whole-cell and nucleus preparations sample different material and can recover different populations. Barcodes label captured profiles rather than certifying one intact cell; quality, ambient RNA and doublet checks remain necessary. Sparse capture and selective recovery prevent a complete census, and many profiles from one biopsy do not create independent patient replicates.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A barcode identifies a captured reaction profile, requiring checks for ambient RNA and multiple contributing cells. Whole-cell and isolated-nucleus preparations sample different compartments; recovered profiles are not a complete tissue census. A zero count does not establish biological absence. Sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28091601/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33367645/.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A barcode labels a reaction compartment and a UMI separates captured molecules from amplified copies, giving a gene-by-barcode table; a barcode does not guarantee one intact cell.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Name the counting unit and normalisation denominator. Estimated transcript counts, length-adjusted transcripts per million and tagged molecule counts answer different measurement questions. A gene total can conceal splice products; pooled RNA does not directly measure surface protein, pathway flux or drug dependence. Sources: https://salmon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/file_formats.html and https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-0881-8.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Record compatible viable/frozen/fixed preparation, material used, chemistry, cell/nucleus recovery and quality/identity checks. Report a gene-by-barcode table with its UMI/read/probe counting unit. Cell calling, low-quality and doublet criteria are chemistry/version-specific. Selective recovery, sparse capture, ambient RNA, degradation and batch require validation; a platform name provides neither a complete census nor clinical validity.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Background correction estimates which part of a profile comes from free RNA in the preparation. SoupX's authors discuss deliberately overcorrecting contamination at the cost of removing a small amount of genuine signal. The estimated contamination and settings therefore need review; a corrected weak count or zero is not an infallible label of the molecule's origin.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A detection fraction uses the analysed profiles and a stated detection rule: it is not automatically the fraction of all cells in the original tissue. A profile with one immune-gene count but otherwise epithelial features is not thereby identified as an immune cell. Sparse recovery, ambient RNA and more than one contributing cell can complicate its interpretation. Check coherent marker evidence and the method of assignment; a mixture of markers does not by itself establish a new cell type. Pooling the counts from a selected set of profiles is pseudobulk. Five hundred nuclei from one biopsy can summarize that selected population, while the biopsy remains one biological specimen rather than five hundred independent patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A larger raw count can be a smaller share of a library. In an invented example, ten captured counts out of 10,000 give 1,000 counts per million, while twenty out of 100,000 give 200. Keep the counted unit and library-size definition. Counts per million scale by that denominator; transcripts per million also use transcript-length information under the chosen quantification method. These relative scales are not interchangeable, do not recover the total RNA made per cell and are not protein counts. A base-two log fold change of plus one corresponds to a ratio of two, and plus two to four under the stated normalization. A reference near zero can make a ratio large while the underlying signal remains small; these are mathematical examples, not biological cutoffs.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An expression-program score has meaning within its algorithm and background. For a score formed by subtracting matched control-gene expression, zero need not mean that no program genes were detected. The 90th percentile places a result relative to a specified reference; it does not mean that 90 percent of cells express the program or that a pathway is 90 percent active. Changing the genes, preprocessing, controls or reference can change the scale, so retain them with the method and version.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Now suppose a group of 500 nuclei from one biopsy is pooled computationally. That is **pseudobulk**. sourceRefs.exactPassage: A **haplotype** is a group of nearby variants carried together on a chromosome. **Phasing** assigns variants to chromosome copies. It can help answer whether two changes lie on the same side. It is different from estimating the fraction of cancer cells carrying a change.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A haplotype groups linked sequence variants on a chromosome that tend to be inherited together. Phasing assigns variants to chromosome copies; that is different from counting carrier cancer cells. Labels A and B distinguish sequence versions without grading either as harmful or harmless. In a fictional set of 100 cancer cells, two variants each present in forty cells could occupy the same forty or separate groups of forty. The two individual fractions do not reveal their overlap. Joint sequence or cell-resolved evidence addresses co-occurrence, with its own sampling limits. Neither shared prevalence nor physical phase alone establishes a variant's functional importance.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: [Human leukocyte antigen loss of heterozygosity (HLA-LOH)](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/sequencing-basics/hla-loh) applies this copy question to antigen-presentation loci. Loss of one inherited HLA version does not establish absent surface expression or complete loss of presentation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:hla: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:hla: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: [**Purity and ploidy**](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/sequencing-basics/variant-allele-fraction-and-cancer-cell-fraction) belong to a stated mixture model. Cell purity is the fraction of cells that are malignant; their DNA contribution can differ because they carry different numbers of copies. **Ploidy** describes genome copy content; a tumor report often gives an average across the genome. Whole-genome doubling can be followed by losses and gains, so a later genome is not a neat four-copy book.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Purity estimates and ploidy fits belong to the tested region and method. A pathology estimate of malignant-cell proportion and a sequencing model fit can disagree. Ploidy is a genome-wide average; local copy number can differ. Several purity-ploidy combinations may explain similar data.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Purity describes the malignant-cell share of the sampled cell mixture; a DNA-based estimate must account for how many genome copies the cells contribute. Ploidy is the average cancer-cell genome copy number. The marble-mixture analogy stops where local copy number and subclonal differences make each cell contribution unequal.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: ASCAT reported aneuploidy above 2.7 genome copies in 45% of its early breast cancer series and near-triploid basal-like genomes consistent with loss followed by duplication. A separate advanced-cancer study identified whole-genome doubling in nearly 30% of 9,692 patients. These populations are different. A region with three copies can be a relative loss against a four-copy baseline, while exceeding a normal diploid count.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: **DNA can suggest a disrupted message. RNA tests the message, protein tests the product, and a controlled assay tests current repair function.**

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

An intronic DNA base may be removed during processing, so a mature-junction read need not contain that base. Assigning the product to a particular allele needs suitable linking sequence or another justified allele-specific measurement, with cell-source and reference checks. RNA directly examines the processing product; the gene-level count cannot settle the protein-function question.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Identify the reference sequence, including its version when the reference database uses versions. For an intronic change, HGVS uses a genomic reference together with the specified transcript used for coding coordinates; a mature transcript reference alone does not contain the intron. The c. prefix gives coding-DNA coordinates and p. describes a protein consequence. The DNA name alone does not specify an exon skip, frameshift or remaining function; one DNA change can produce several RNA products.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: [DNA damage and repair](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/genome-instability-and-repair/dna-damage-and-repair-overview) includes double-strand breaks, where both strands of the DNA backbone are broken. [Homologous recombination (HR)](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/genome-instability-and-repair/homologous-recombination-and-hrd) repairs certain DNA breaks using a matching template; homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) describes impaired function. A [genomic scar](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/genome-instability-and-repair/genomic-scars) records accumulated damage history, which can differ from present function.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A composite score compresses selected features of a tumour's chromosome history. Like a summary of past events, it leaves details out; like numbers on differently calibrated scales, the same numerical value need not have the same meaning in two laboratories. The composite count is not a percentage of repair-deficient cells. Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity can replace two parental versions with copies of one version without reducing the total copy number, so loss of heterozygosity is not always loss of a physical chromosome copy.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The specimen and analysis are part of the result. Telli used tumour DNA, a genome-wide SNP panel, allele-imbalance profiles and prespecified counting rules; if the score failed and BRCA testing was negative or failed, HRD status was undetermined. A failed result is not a low score. Reports should identify the assay version, usable tumour content, DNA input/quality, copy-number and allele-balance method, segmentation, and purity/ploidy assumptions. HRDetect was explored in a small biopsy series and one formalin-fixed specimen with substantial sequencing artefact; those demonstrations do not certify every degraded specimen. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
RAD51 nuclear foci are assemblies of a protein involved in homologous recombination. Their interpretation depends on the sampled tumour cells, cell-cycle state, damage, staining, scoring and controls. A low count without enough informative cycling cells is uninformative rather than proof that repair is absent. The assay is a functional surrogate, not direct observation of every completed repair event.

Cruz and colleagues in 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived breast cancer models and retrospective tumour specimens. Castroviejo-Bermejo and colleagues separately compared RAD51 and genomic HRD scores against olaparib response in breast cancer xenografts, then assessed feasibility in archival breast samples, including PALB2-related cancers. The latter clinical samples established feasibility, rather than a randomised benefit from choosing treatment with the assay.

A scar records accumulated genomic changes; a suitably controlled RAD51 result asks about a present repair-related state. Repair-restoring changes and acquired foci were observed in selected resistant BRCA-mutated breast cancers, but those small cohorts do not establish a universal treatment-switch rule. Use the actual assay version, informative-cell requirements and intended-use validation. A research score cannot replace the biomarker, disease and companion-test conditions of a medicine's label.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: A fictional repair gene has a splice-site change. RNA shows an abnormal junction. That strengthens the message-processing claim. Tissue staining then shows reduced R signal in malignant cells. That adds a cell-specific protein observation, but does not establish whether intact R remains: the answer depends on which forms the antibody and assay distinguish. Finally, a controlled repair assay indicates impaired repair in a suitable model.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

A reproducible abnormal junction supports a local RNA join, rather than a complete transcript, its protein or its originating DNA allele. An intronic DNA base may be removed during processing, so a mature-junction read need not contain that base. Assigning the product to a particular allele needs suitable linking sequence or another justified allele-specific measurement, with cell-source and reference checks. RNA directly examines the processing product; the gene-level count cannot settle the protein-function question.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: - Calling every exon skip a frameshift.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
RAD51 nuclear foci are assemblies of a protein involved in homologous recombination. Their interpretation depends on the sampled tumour cells, cell-cycle state, damage, staining, scoring and controls. A low count without enough informative cycling cells is uninformative rather than proof that repair is absent. The assay is a functional surrogate, not direct observation of every completed repair event.

Cruz and colleagues in 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived breast cancer models and retrospective tumour specimens. Castroviejo-Bermejo and colleagues separately compared RAD51 and genomic HRD scores against olaparib response in breast cancer xenografts, then assessed feasibility in archival breast samples, including PALB2-related cancers. The latter clinical samples established feasibility, rather than a randomised benefit from choosing treatment with the assay.

A scar records accumulated genomic changes; a suitably controlled RAD51 result asks about a present repair-related state. Repair-restoring changes and acquired foci were observed in selected resistant BRCA-mutated breast cancers, but those small cohorts do not establish a universal treatment-switch rule. Use the actual assay version, informative-cell requirements and intended-use validation. A research score cannot replace the biomarker, disease and companion-test conditions of a medicine's label.

points.heading: Explain it back
points.requirement: One answer: “what might happen; what message was made; accumulated repair history; current behavior under its conditions.”

sourceRefs.exactPassage: One answer: “what might happen; what message was made; accumulated repair history; current behavior under its conditions.”

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.
