coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Splicing joins exons and removes introns. A variant at a splice boundary raises a processing question that only RNA can answer.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Splicing processes an initial RNA transcript. Exons are retained in a specified product and may contain untranslated sequence; introns are removed. For many nuclear pre-mRNAs, a spliceosome made of RNA and proteins recognizes boundary and regulatory sequences. The donor site starts an intron and the acceptor site ends it. Alternative choices yield transcript isoforms; a variant can alter exon inclusion, intron retention or use of a cryptic site. Exon skipping is not automatically a frameshift: the coding sequence and resulting joins matter. An altered message may undergo nonsense-mediated decay or produce a changed protein, but neither outcome follows from a prediction alone.

Cancer-associated splicing changes can arise through altered RNA-processing factors or their expression. SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ZRSR2 illustrate studied factors; AR-V7 and BCL2L1 illustrate named transcript contexts. The linked review describes disease-specific mechanisms and therapeutic research. An altered transcript alone does not establish an intact abnormal protein, immune presentation, a therapeutic dependency or patient benefit. Free-drug development and a conjugated payload also require their own construct-specific evidence.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rna-splicing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional repair-gene example, a high gene-level RNA count can include abnormal splice products and messages from normal neighbours. A reproducible abnormal junction supports a local RNA join, rather than a complete transcript, its protein or its originating DNA allele. An intronic DNA base may be removed during processing, so a mature-junction read need not contain that base. Assigning the product to a particular allele needs suitable linking sequence or another justified allele-specific measurement, with cell-source and reference checks. RNA directly examines the processing product; the gene-level count cannot settle the protein-function question.

The DNA name alone does not specify an exon skip, frameshift or remaining function; one DNA change can produce several RNA products.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Perou and colleagues profiled 65 surgical specimens from 42 patients on cDNA microarrays of 8,102 genes and found the tumours could be classified into subtypes distinguished by pervasive differences in gene expression, the origin of the intrinsic subtypes luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like and normal-like (Perou 2000). The Cancer Genome Atlas integrated copy number, methylation, exome, mRNA, microRNA and protein data across primary breast cancers, confirmed four main classes, found TP53, PIK3CA and GATA3 the only genes mutated in more than 10 percent overall, and showed basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, implying a related aetiology and similar therapeutic opportunities (TCGA 2012). Triple-negative and basal-like overlap but are not identical: of 412 triple-negative tumours 21.4 percent were non-basal-like, and of 473 basal-like tumours 31.5 percent were not triple-negative; triple-negative tumours classified as luminal or HER2-enriched had expression profiles indistinguishable from their non-triple-negative counterparts, most HER2-enriched triple-negative tumours lacked HER2 amplification, and the authors suggest triple-negative trials stratify by basal-like versus non-basal-like expression (Prat 2013). In the population-based Carolina Breast Cancer Study, using immunohistochemical surrogates (ER, PR and HER2 negative with cytokeratin 5/6 or HER1 positive), basal-like tumours were found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 14 percent of postmenopausal African American and 16 percent of non-African American women; they had more TP53 mutations (44 against 15 percent), higher mitotic index and grade, and among the shortest breast cancer-specific survival (Carey 2006). Basal-like cancers are the typical cancer of BRCA1 carriers, and adenoid cystic carcinoma is a special type of basal-like tumour with an excellent outlook (Ghabach 2010), a reminder that an expression label does not establish a uniform behaviour or exact cell ancestry. PAM50 basal-like and Lehmann BL1/BL2 belong to different classifiers; a PAM50 basal-like call does not by itself assign either Lehmann profile.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Perou and colleagues profiled 65 surgical specimens from 42 patients on cDNA microarrays of 8,102 genes and found the tumours could be classified into subtypes distinguished by pervasive differences in gene expression, the origin of the intrinsic subtypes luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like and normal-like (Perou 2000). The Cancer Genome Atlas integrated copy number, methylation, exome, mRNA, microRNA and protein data across primary breast cancers, confirmed four main classes, found TP53, PIK3CA and GATA3 the only genes mutated in more than 10 percent overall, and showed basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, implying a related aetiology and similar therapeutic opportunities (TCGA 2012). Triple-negative and basal-like overlap but are not identical: of 412 triple-negative tumours 21.4 percent were non-basal-like, and of 473 basal-like tumours 31.5 percent were not triple-negative; triple-negative tumours classified as luminal or HER2-enriched had expression profiles indistinguishable from their non-triple-negative counterparts, most HER2-enriched triple-negative tumours lacked HER2 amplification, and the authors suggest triple-negative trials stratify by basal-like versus non-basal-like expression (Prat 2013). In the population-based Carolina Breast Cancer Study, using immunohistochemical surrogates (ER, PR and HER2 negative with cytokeratin 5/6 or HER1 positive), basal-like tumours were found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 14 percent of postmenopausal African American and 16 percent of non-African American women; they had more TP53 mutations (44 against 15 percent), higher mitotic index and grade, and among the shortest breast cancer-specific survival (Carey 2006). Basal-like cancers are the typical cancer of BRCA1 carriers, and adenoid cystic carcinoma is a special type of basal-like tumour with an excellent outlook (Ghabach 2010), a reminder that an expression label does not establish a uniform behaviour or exact cell ancestry. PAM50 basal-like and Lehmann BL1/BL2 belong to different classifiers; a PAM50 basal-like call does not by itself assign either Lehmann profile.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Mass-spectrometry and antibody-based methods measure different protein-derived signals under defined workflows. A primary yeast study measured protein expression alongside phosphorylation and showed why a changed phosphopeptide signal can reflect protein abundance as well as phosphorylation. That methodological result is not a validated cancer-treatment rule. Targeted plasma-protein assays likewise require evidence about recovery, calibration and quantitative range. A protein measurement, modification-site signal, functional pathway dependence and prediction of treatment benefit are distinct claims. Beausoleil and colleagues introduced the Ascore, a probability-based score for how likely a phosphorylation site is correctly localised from site-determining ions in tandem mass spectra, alongside a target-decoy measure of dataset error (2006). In yeast, 25 per cent of seemingly differential phosphopeptides were attributable to changes in protein expression once phosphopeptide ratios were calibrated by protein levels (Wu and colleagues, 2011). In human ovarian tumour and breast cancer xenograft tissue collected without vascular interruption, rapid phosphorylation changes were seen in up to 24 per cent of the phosphoproteome after defined ischaemic intervals, while the global proteome and most of more than 25,000 quantified phosphosites were unchanged after 60 minutes; phosphopeptides in that study were enriched by immobilised metal (Fe3+) affinity chromatography before analysis (Mertins and colleagues, 2014).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

points.heading: A worked finding: HER2-low as a delivery address
points.requirement: Carry every factual, numeric, causal and interpretive clause, or an explicit supported correction. Exact field containment alone cannot establish semantic acceptance.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: HER2-positive cancers depend on HER2 signaling, and HER2-blocking antibodies treat them. A much larger group of breast cancers carries only a little HER2 on the membrane: IHC 1+, or 2+ without gene amplification on ISH. These **HER2-low** tumors are classed as HER2-negative, and many are also triple-negative.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
HER2-low generally denotes IHC 1+ or IHC 2+ with a negative ISH result in the relevant breast-cancer context. HER2-ultralow denotes the IHC 0 pattern with membrane staining used in DESTINY-Breast06 and the corresponding U.S. ENHERTU label. These are measured categories with assay and reporting context. The September 2026 CAP template records the membrane-staining pattern as negative score 0+, separately from negative score 0 with no detected membrane staining.

DESTINY-Breast04 studied previously chemotherapy-treated HER2-low metastatic disease, including hormone receptor-positive and hormone receptor-negative participants. DESTINY-Breast06 studied hormone receptor-positive disease after endocrine therapy without prior chemotherapy for metastatic disease; its primary comparison concerned HER2-low disease and its ultralow analysis was exploratory. Neither trial establishes that every low-expression category is one biological disease or validates a cutoff for every ADC. The U.S. ENHERTU HER2-low and HER2-ultralow breast indications require an FDA-authorized HER2 test and unresectable or metastatic disease. One use is HR-positive HER2-low or HER2-ultralow disease that has progressed on one or more endocrine therapies in the metastatic setting. A separate HER2-low use requires prior chemotherapy in the metastatic setting, or recurrence during or within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy. The latter low-expression use does not require HR-positive disease; the ultralow indication does. The score alone does not establish eligibility or individual benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Total copy count, allele identity, RNA abundance and protein activity are separate measurements. Purity, ploidy and the assay’s definition affect copy calls. Fehrmann and colleagues related copy number to expression after modelling shared transcriptional components in large datasets; that association does not promise a fixed protein increase, target dependence or treatment benefit in a particular tumour.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
DESTINY-Breast04 (NCT03734029) randomised 557 patients with HER2-low metastatic breast cancer after one or two prior lines of chemotherapy: 494 were hormone receptor-positive and 63 hormone receptor-negative at randomisation. HER2-low meant IHC 1+ or IHC 2+/ISH-negative. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival in the hormone receptor-positive cohort; key secondary endpoints included overall-population progression-free survival and overall survival. The 2022 report showed longer progression-free and overall survival with trastuzumab deruxtecan.

The study did not randomize IHC 0 tumours and does not establish a universal HER2-expression floor, biological category or eligibility for everyone with HER2-negative disease. Exploratory hormone receptor-negative analyses use their specified efficacy populations, distinct from the randomised stratification count. The later Nature Medicine report and current drug label are separate dated sources, not interchangeable versions of the original result.

In the DESTINY-Breast04 trial (557 people with previously treated HER2-low metastatic breast cancer), median progression-free survival was 9.9 months with trastuzumab deruxtecan and 5.1 months with chemotherapy of the physician's choice, and median overall survival 23.4 versus 16.8 months ([Modi et al., 2022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35665782/)). sourceRefs.exactPassage: The result changed what a stain had to distinguish. HER2 IHC was built to separate overexpression (3+) from the rest, not 0 from 1+. When 18 pathologists scored the same set of 170 breast cancer biopsies, concordance between 0 and 1+ was only 26%, against 58% between 2+ and 3+ ([Fernandez et al., 2022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35113160/)). A protein measurement is only as useful as its validation for the decision it now supports.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Fernandez and colleagues selected 170 biopsies, enriched for two-plus and three-plus cases, for eighteen pathologists to score. Ninety-two cases were called zero by at least one reader; twenty-four of those reached agreement by at least seventeen readers, about 26 percent. Of forty-five cases called three-plus by at least one reader, twenty-six reached that agreement, about 58 percent. These are case-level consensus proportions in separately defined groups, not pairwise agreement percentages or measured sensitivity and specificity. The readers were not told that zero versus one-plus agreement was the particular question.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The Yale analysis used a case-level agreement rule: at least seventeen of eighteen readers had to give one score. The denominators depended on whether any reader called a case zero or three-plus. This measures reader agreement in a selected experiment, rather than accuracy against an independently known truth or the chance that an individual result is wrong. Its historical treatment context does not define current eligibility.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Two more lessons follow. Abundance is not dependence: a delivery target need not drive growth, and a signaling inhibitor needs pathway behavior, not surface density. And a gene-level signal does not identify every protein **isoform**, or molecular version; normal-tissue expression and access remain part of the [drug mechanism](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/how-drugs-work/drug-target-and-mechanism).

A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
HER2-low generally denotes IHC 1+ or IHC 2+ with a negative ISH result in the relevant breast-cancer context. HER2-ultralow denotes the IHC 0 pattern with membrane staining used in DESTINY-Breast06 and the corresponding U.S. ENHERTU label. These are measured categories with assay and reporting context. The September 2026 CAP template records the membrane-staining pattern as negative score 0+, separately from negative score 0 with no detected membrane staining.

DESTINY-Breast04 studied previously chemotherapy-treated HER2-low metastatic disease, including hormone receptor-positive and hormone receptor-negative participants. DESTINY-Breast06 studied hormone receptor-positive disease after endocrine therapy without prior chemotherapy for metastatic disease; its primary comparison concerned HER2-low disease and its ultralow analysis was exploratory. Neither trial establishes that every low-expression category is one biological disease or validates a cutoff for every ADC. The U.S. ENHERTU HER2-low and HER2-ultralow breast indications require an FDA-authorized HER2 test and unresectable or metastatic disease. One use is HR-positive HER2-low or HER2-ultralow disease that has progressed on one or more endocrine therapies in the metastatic setting. A separate HER2-low use requires prior chemotherapy in the metastatic setting, or recurrence during or within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy. The latter low-expression use does not require HR-positive disease; the ultralow indication does. The score alone does not establish eligibility or individual benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: An epitope is a molecular feature recognised by an immune receptor; its definition depends on the receptor and the tested molecular preparation. Trastuzumab and pertuzumab both bind HER2 but at different epitopes, which is why they can be given together, and zanidatamab is a single antibody built to grab both spots at once. For T cells, the epitope is a short peptide fragment held in an HLA molecule on the cell surface; an alteration that changes recognition can permit escape, but its effects on processing, display and other cell functions need their own evidence. The epitope an antibody recognises can be a continuous stretch of sequence or a surface formed by folding, so distant parts of the chain can meet; accessibility matters, and binding to an isolated protein does not show the same site is reachable on an intact cell. For a conventional T-cell receptor the target is the peptide together with the restricting HLA molecule, and the same peptide on another HLA molecule is a different recognition surface.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
RAD51 nuclear foci are assemblies of a protein involved in homologous recombination. Their interpretation depends on the sampled tumour cells, cell-cycle state, damage, staining, scoring and controls. A low count without enough informative cycling cells is uninformative rather than proof that repair is absent. The assay is a functional surrogate, not direct observation of every completed repair event.

Cruz and colleagues in 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived breast cancer models and retrospective tumour specimens. Castroviejo-Bermejo and colleagues separately compared RAD51 and genomic HRD scores against olaparib response in breast cancer xenografts, then assessed feasibility in archival breast samples, including PALB2-related cancers. The latter clinical samples established feasibility, rather than a randomised benefit from choosing treatment with the assay.

A scar records accumulated genomic changes; a suitably controlled RAD51 result asks about a present repair-related state. Repair-restoring changes and acquired foci were observed in selected resistant BRCA-mutated breast cancers, but those small cohorts do not establish a universal treatment-switch rule. Use the actual assay version, informative-cell requirements and intended-use validation. A research score cannot replace the biomarker, disease and companion-test conditions of a medicine's label.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: [Immunopeptidomics](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/proteins-and-spatial/immunopeptidomics) asks a different protein-related question: which peptides were recovered from human leukocyte antigen complexes? Presentation is closer to an immune-target question than total gene expression, but does not establish recognition by itself.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A primary melanoma study used mass spectrometry to identify HLA-associated peptides from native tumor tissue and then evaluated selected mutated peptides with immune assays. This is stronger evidence of natural presentation in the sampled material than a binding prediction alone. The analytical observation still has a defined specimen and workflow. It does not automatically establish the abundance of a ligand on every cancer cell, receptor recognition or a treatment effect. A published protocol isolates MHC-peptide complexes by immunoaffinity capture, dissociates the peptides by acid denaturation, fractionates them by HPLC and identifies them by nano-UPLC tandem mass spectrometry, from cell lines and tissues (Purcell and colleagues, 2019). Capture starts from mild-detergent solubilised lysates (Chong and colleagues, 2018; Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020 immunoprecipitated HLA from soluble lysates), so a lysate is not a surface-only survey, and in multi-allele samples a peptide was assigned to the best-scoring allele or alleles by computation (Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020). Identification depends on the analysis: a deep-learning model trained on more than 300,000 synthetic peptides improved HLA peptide identification up to 7-fold and indicated that 87 per cent of the proposed proteasomally spliced HLA peptides may be incorrect (Wilhelm and colleagues, 2021). A quantitative tissue study isolated peptide-HLA complexes from snap-frozen tissue and used formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded blocks only for histology (Science Translational Medicine, 2022).

A signal detected below the quantification limit is meaningful as detection, but it does not support a reliable amount, and neither it nor non-detection means biological zero. coverageEvidence.excerpt: Assay card in words (a reading guide). Measures and how: selected peptide amounts, by extracting, digesting, measuring specified ions and fragments with controls, calibrating and assessing analyte performance. Input and tissue cost: a validated tissue, cell or fluid matrix; extraction and digestion consume material, and required mass or volume and fixation compatibility are assay-specific. Output and units: peptide identity, amount or ratio, with the denominator and the peptide-to-protein inference kept. Thresholds: analyte-specific limit of detection, quantification limit, upper limit, bias and precision acceptance and reportable range, with no universal limit or treatment threshold. Failure modes: incomplete recovery or digestion, shared peptides, interference, unstable standards, matrix effects and signal outside the validated range. Limits: no automatic intact-form, location, cell-of-origin, accessibility, occupancy or drug-dependence conclusion. Validation tier: fit-for-purpose research tiers describe analytical characterisation and do not themselves confer clinical approval.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. Simoni found bystander CD8 cells recognizing viral rather than cancer epitopes in human lung and colorectal tumours; the study’s CD39 associations are not a universal test of every cell’s target. A functional assay compares defined effectors and targets with recognition and target-survival controls. Neither presence, cytokine release nor one killing assay reproduces every access barrier or establishes clinical benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:t-cell-receptor: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A list of cell types is a roster and not a functional report: a cell-family name does not show what a cell is doing, a marker shared by several populations is not a complete identity test (single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes; Villani et al., 2017), and a fraction of immune cells depends on its denominator (percent of recovered immune cells, of T cells and of all tissue cells are different quantities). Blood composition does not substitute for tumour composition, and a count of immune cells in a tumour does not by itself show recognition or killing. CD4 and CD8 are co-receptors and not permanent helper and killer assignments, tumour-associated macrophage names a setting, myeloid-derived suppressor cells need an operational phenotype and a test of suppressive function, and natural killer T cells are a T-cell family distinct from natural killer cells despite the name. In the classical description innate immunity is rapid and without immunologic memory while adaptive immunity is antigen-specific with a capacity for memory, and the two are not mutually exclusive (Marshall et al., 2018). Cytotoxic CD4 T cells have been found in infections, tumours and inflammatory disease, so a CD4 or CD8 label does not fix a helper or killer role (Venkatesh et al., 2023), and a myeloid-derived suppressor cell label rests on myeloid origin plus shown suppressive function (Bronte et al., 2016). CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors for T-cell receptors that recognise MHC, and a review discusses how they help impose MHC specificity during thymic selection (Van Laethem et al., 2012), so a CD4 or CD8 label names a coreceptor and not a job.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: External evaluation applies an existing model to data outside its development and compares predictions with observed outcomes. The TRIPOD-Cluster explanation includes later-period data collected by the same investigators as well as data from another hospital, country or care setting. A different platform is not a universal requirement. Apparent performance uses the development data and can be optimistic. Internal validation with resampling can estimate optimism and performance for new people from the same source population; it is evidence about a different question, rather than no result. External evaluation quantifies performance and its uncertainty instead of conferring a universal pass or fail. Keep the locked method, population, outcome, follow-up and differences from development visible.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: The next question might concern access, presentation or clinical association. It should not become an automatic instruction to add a treatment. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are lymphocytes found in sampled tumour tissue, including T- and B-cell populations. The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by a defined mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within eligible tumour-associated stroma on H&E sections. Higher pretreatment scores were associated with better outcomes in the cited early triple-negative breast cancer cohorts, but those associations do not guarantee an individual outcome or establish extra benefit from pembrolizumab. Intratumoral location, stromal area, immune-cell counts and cells expanded for TIL therapy are different measurements or uses.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A useful IHC result identifies the block, fixation and section, antibody clone, retrieval and detection system, eligible cells and scored compartment. Cutting and staining use finite tissue. Report the percentage, intensity, location and named scoring scale, together with expected-positive tissue, relevant internal controls and background assessment. Poor preservation, nonspecific binding, few eligible cells, heterogeneous staining and observer variation can limit interpretation. Validation must fit the assay and its intended use; a research measurement is not automatically a clinical selection test.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A list of cell types is a roster and not a functional report: a cell-family name does not show what a cell is doing, a marker shared by several populations is not a complete identity test (single-cell sequencing of human blood found six dendritic-cell and four monocyte subtypes; Villani et al., 2017), and a fraction of immune cells depends on its denominator (percent of recovered immune cells, of T cells and of all tissue cells are different quantities). Blood composition does not substitute for tumour composition, and a count of immune cells in a tumour does not by itself show recognition or killing. CD4 and CD8 are co-receptors and not permanent helper and killer assignments, tumour-associated macrophage names a setting, myeloid-derived suppressor cells need an operational phenotype and a test of suppressive function, and natural killer T cells are a T-cell family distinct from natural killer cells despite the name. In the classical description innate immunity is rapid and without immunologic memory while adaptive immunity is antigen-specific with a capacity for memory, and the two are not mutually exclusive (Marshall et al., 2018). Cytotoxic CD4 T cells have been found in infections, tumours and inflammatory disease, so a CD4 or CD8 label does not fix a helper or killer role (Venkatesh et al., 2023), and a myeloid-derived suppressor cell label rests on myeloid origin plus shown suppressive function (Bronte et al., 2016). CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors for T-cell receptors that recognise MHC, and a review discusses how they help impose MHC specificity during thymic selection (Van Laethem et al., 2012), so a CD4 or CD8 label names a coreceptor and not a job.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Assay card for multiplex immunofluorescence (a reading guide, not a score). Input and tissue cost: a compatible fixed or frozen section; staining uses material and may involve repeated processing, and the section does not preserve viable cells for a killing assay. Output and units: marker images, fluorescence intensity in assay-dependent units, cell counts, cells per square millimetre, cell fractions and defined distances in micrometres. Controls: marker-positive and marker-negative material, comparison with validated single-marker staining, channel or spectral controls, background assessment, cycle alignment and boundary overlays. Thresholds: panel-specific marker and phenotype rules locked before the intended comparison and tested for reproducibility. Failure modes: autofluorescence, overlapping signals, nonspecific antibodies, staining-order effects, tissue loss, alignment errors and incorrect cell boundaries. Cannot establish: all proteins, live-cell behaviour, antigen specificity, actual killing or universal treatment eligibility. Validation: specific to the panel, staining, imaging, analysis and intended use.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:multiplex-immunofluorescence: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A primary melanoma study used mass spectrometry to identify HLA-associated peptides from native tumor tissue and then evaluated selected mutated peptides with immune assays. This is stronger evidence of natural presentation in the sampled material than a binding prediction alone. The analytical observation still has a defined specimen and workflow. It does not automatically establish the abundance of a ligand on every cancer cell, receptor recognition or a treatment effect. A published protocol isolates MHC-peptide complexes by immunoaffinity capture, dissociates the peptides by acid denaturation, fractionates them by HPLC and identifies them by nano-UPLC tandem mass spectrometry, from cell lines and tissues (Purcell and colleagues, 2019). Capture starts from mild-detergent solubilised lysates (Chong and colleagues, 2018; Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020 immunoprecipitated HLA from soluble lysates), so a lysate is not a surface-only survey, and in multi-allele samples a peptide was assigned to the best-scoring allele or alleles by computation (Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020). Identification depends on the analysis: a deep-learning model trained on more than 300,000 synthetic peptides improved HLA peptide identification up to 7-fold and indicated that 87 per cent of the proposed proteasomally spliced HLA peptides may be incorrect (Wilhelm and colleagues, 2021). A quantitative tissue study isolated peptide-HLA complexes from snap-frozen tissue and used formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded blocks only for histology (Science Translational Medicine, 2022).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Functional drug testing exposes a defined living preparation to medicines and measures a specified response. Preparations may use dissociated cells, expanded organoids or short-term tissue cultures. Feasibility, outcome agreement and benefit from using a result to choose care are separate questions and must be tied to the actual assay version, cancer, treatment and setting.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: A conventional [T-cell receptor](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/t-cell-receptor) reads a peptide displayed on [human leukocyte antigen (HLA)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/antigen-presentation/hla). coverageEvidence.excerpt: In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:hla: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Assay card for spatial transcriptomics (a reading guide, not a score). Measures and how: RNA with coordinates, by preparing a section, capturing or probing RNA, sequencing or imaging, decoding, registering positions and reporting the assignment rules. Input and tissue cost: protocol-compatible frozen or fixed sections; sectioning and molecular preparation consume allocated material, some workflows alter or destroy the assayed section, and re-scoring existing data consumes no new tissue. Output and units: gene counts per spot, bin or assigned cell, and decoded molecule coordinates, often in micrometres, with physical dimensions, normalisation and observed-versus-imputed labels kept. Thresholds: assay-specific gene or probe coverage, capture and decoding quality, background and segmentation criteria; no universal high-expression or neighbourhood cutoff. Failure modes: poor RNA, incomplete probe coverage, low capture, image-registration errors, inaccurate segmentation, spillover and unsuitable reference models. Limits: no automatic single-cell identity, complete transcriptome, whole-tumour representation, proven interaction or clinical selection rule. Validation tier: many workflows are research methods, so check analytical and intended-use validation for the exact assay and model; resolution claims and regulatory status are separate questions.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:spatial-transcriptomics: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Figure reading (fictional geometry, no platform scale): a capture spot is one barcode that can pool several cells. Imaging decodes six RNA coordinates, three for gene G and three for gene H (3 + 3 = 6), and these are coordinates, not cell labels. Moving the estimated cell masks changes which cell a coordinate is assigned to while the RNA stays fixed. Gene R is absent from the G and H panel, so a model-inferred R value is not an observed molecule, and RNA position is not protein or function.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A larger raw count can be a smaller share of a library. In an invented example, ten captured counts out of 10,000 give 1,000 counts per million, while twenty out of 100,000 give 200. Keep the counted unit and library-size definition. Counts per million scale by that denominator; transcripts per million also use transcript-length information under the chosen quantification method. These relative scales are not interchangeable, do not recover the total RNA made per cell and are not protein counts. A base-two log fold change of plus one corresponds to a ratio of two, and plus two to four under the stated normalization. A reference near zero can make a ratio large while the underlying signal remains small; these are mathematical examples, not biological cutoffs.
