sourceRefs.exactPassage: Tissue staining places R on cancer-cell membranes. That adds localization, but normal-organ access and expression still matter. In a model, blocking R has little effect on growth. R may be a possible delivery address for an antibody–drug conjugate, a medicine that carries a payload through an antibody, as HER2-low is in [the protein lesson](/wiki/education/guides/what-multi-omics-tells-us/06-read-protein#a-worked-finding-her2-low-as-a-delivery-address). R could be investigated as an antibody-drug-conjugate delivery address, but that hypothesis still needs evidence for binding, access, uptake where required, payload effect and relevant normal-tissue exposure. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
HER2-low generally denotes IHC 1+ or IHC 2+ with a negative ISH result in the relevant breast-cancer context. HER2-ultralow denotes the IHC 0 pattern with membrane staining used in DESTINY-Breast06 and the corresponding U.S. ENHERTU label. These are measured categories with assay and reporting context. The September 2026 CAP template records the membrane-staining pattern as negative score 0+, separately from negative score 0 with no detected membrane staining.

DESTINY-Breast04 studied previously chemotherapy-treated HER2-low metastatic disease, including hormone receptor-positive and hormone receptor-negative participants. DESTINY-Breast06 studied hormone receptor-positive disease after endocrine therapy without prior chemotherapy for metastatic disease; its primary comparison concerned HER2-low disease and its ultralow analysis was exploratory. Neither trial establishes that every low-expression category is one biological disease or validates a cutoff for every ADC. The U.S. ENHERTU HER2-low and HER2-ultralow breast indications require an FDA-authorized HER2 test and unresectable or metastatic disease. One use is HR-positive HER2-low or HER2-ultralow disease that has progressed on one or more endocrine therapies in the metastatic setting. A separate HER2-low use requires prior chemotherapy in the metastatic setting, or recurrence during or within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy. The latter low-expression use does not require HR-positive disease; the ultralow indication does. The score alone does not establish eligibility or individual benefit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

points.heading: Count independent observations, not reports
points.requirement: Carry every factual, numeric, causal and interpretive clause, or an explicit supported correction. Exact field containment alone cannot establish semantic acceptance.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Several reports can share one tissue sample, one variant list or one analysis pipeline. Agreement among them shows consistency, not independent confirmation. The DNA lesson explains why a caller's PASS flag or agreement between callers is [not independent support](/wiki/education/guides/what-multi-omics-tells-us/03-read-dna#audit-the-call-not-just-the-gene-name). The same logic applies across layers: an RNA junction measured separately adds a new observation; a second report that reuses the first DNA call does not.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: **A functional experiment changes one thing and observes the response. Its meaning depends on what the model preserves, what it leaves out and which denominator the result uses.**

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Controlled perturbations deliberately change specified factors and compare responses with suitable controls. A model response alone does not prove its mechanism or patient benefit.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:controlled-perturbation: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Keep what changed, the comparator, concentration or dose range, timing, assignment, readout and units, sample identities, replicate structure and variability. Repeated wells address variation under their preparation and allocation; independently obtained biological samples address another source of variation. Many wells from one tumour do not become independent patients, and repetition or a small p-value does not repair a missing comparison. A two-drug experiment needs vehicle, both single drugs and the combination. A larger combination effect than either single drug is not automatically synergy; that claim needs a stated reference model.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Functional drug testing exposes a defined living preparation to medicines and measures a specified response. coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Fictional direct counts: vehicle-treated cells increase from 100 to 200 while drug-treated cells remain at 100. The endpoint drug count is half the vehicle count without measured net decline from the starting count, so calling it 50 per cent killing overstates the observation. Slower growth, death and a molecular change require their own readouts; direct death or recovery measurements could address further questions. Hafner and colleagues showed that conventional IC50 and maximal-effect measures depend on cell divisions during an assay and developed growth-rate metrics to address that dependence. A real experimental response does not by itself establish the responsible target or clinical benefit.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Suppose earlier layers suggested drug A acts on a repair defect. [Genetic dependency mapping](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/functional-models/dependency-mapping-crispr) could test a related genetic change. Here are invented summaries at 0.3 micromoles per liter: counts are medians of three wells, and mass and metabolic signal come from matched parallel aliquots.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an entirely invented tumour-only organoid experiment from one donor and one characterised preparation, with three wells per condition. Drug A is tested at 0.1, 0.3 and 1 micromoles per litre for 48 hours with matched carrier and handling. The planned primary readout is calibrated viable tumour-cell count at the start and endpoint, with cell identity checked. Vehicle, a positive control with an expected response and a target perturbation or rescue ask different questions. Their actual results must be documented; the illustrative counts do not show that every control passed. Three wells are not three donors. This preparation supplies neither immune cells, full human metabolism nor a healthy-organ toxicity measurement, and these example exposures are not human doses.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Two matched parallel aliquots add different fictional readouts to the same comparison; they do not track the original cells individually. Mean buoyant mass is 20 picograms per measured cell at the start, 21 with vehicle and 16 with treatment, so the treated mean is 80 percent of its starting value. Metabolic signal is 100 arbitrary units at the start, 190 with vehicle and 70 with treatment: 70 divided by 190 is about 36.8 percent, a 63.2 percent reduction relative to vehicle. Neither is a killed-cell fraction. A changing population mean is not an individual-cell trajectory, and buoyant mass depends on cell volume and the difference between cell and fluid density. It is not dry mass, a count of living cells or a measurement of a particular death mechanism.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A suspended microchannel resonator weighs a cell relative to the fluid it displaces using the shift in a vibrating beam's frequency. Buoyant mass equals cell volume multiplied by the difference between cell and fluid density. It is not simply diameter or dry mass. Repeatedly measuring the same cell estimates mass accumulation rate; Godin reversed the flow to reintroduce the same cell to the sensor (a dynamic trap) and Cermak used serial sensors along one channel. Stevens investigated drug-response associations in specified cancer models and leukaemia samples, rather than universal clinical prediction.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Quality and inference. Check clumps, cell attribution, instrument drift, calibration, tracking ambiguity and sufficient linked readings. Serial-sensor analyses exclude uncertain matches rather than invent a trajectory. Fluid-density changes can change buoyant mass. A small positive slope still indicates accumulation in the observed interval; later recovery, death and resistance need additional endpoints and time. Many measured cells from one specimen are not many independent patients. No universal rate cutoff establishes clinical sensitivity or immune recognition. Buoyant mass is also not a count of cell divisions. Physical measurement performance, a reproducible drug-response association and validated use for a clinical decision are separate kinds of evidence. Without extra measurements or assumptions, this sensor does not establish dry mass, a death mechanism, immune specificity or patient benefit.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: A controlled response supports a laboratory hypothesis. It does not establish achievable exposure or patient benefit, and two drugs scoring differently in one well do not justify a regimen switch. For drug combinations and interaction models, use [Read a functional experiment](/wiki/education/guides/from-variant-to-drug/07-reading-a-functional-experiment).

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Functional drug testing exposes a defined living preparation to medicines and measures a specified response. Preparations may use dissociated cells, expanded organoids or short-term tissue cultures. Feasibility, outcome agreement and benefit from using a result to choose care are separate questions and must be tied to the actual assay version, cancer, treatment and setting.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Specimen and assay card. Record donor/site/time, living preparation, transport and processing, initial composition, culture history, assay version, concentrations, exposure duration, replicates and control range. Fixed tissue cannot supply living cells; whether previously frozen material can supply the required viable preparation must be demonstrated for that protocol. Input suitability and recovery must be demonstrated for the method. Testing and endpoint processing use finite material. Output needs units, denominator, normalisation and uncertainty; acceptance criteria must be defined for the actual method. Name whether the preparation is dissociated cells, a fresh fragment or an expanded organoid. Mixed samples include normal neighbours, and expansion can change the represented populations.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Handling evidence is method-specific. Ladan and colleagues collected breast tissue in their specified medium, cut 300 micrometre slices and assessed morphology, proliferation and apoptosis after three-day exposure. This is not a general transport or storage protocol for all screens. Growth-rate methods show why baseline counts and control division affect interpretation. Retain failures and exclusions; failed preparation is not clinical resistance. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4887336/ Medium, drug access and exposure duration can change the result. Mechanism-relevant controls test whether the claimed interaction can occur; absent required cells or unrealistic exposures can make an experiment uninformative even when a numerical response is available. A laboratory concentration is not a safe human dose.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. Eligibility exclusions, absent tumour, laboratory failures, missing outcomes and people not receiving the treatment belong to different steps. State whether the unit is a person, specimen or treatment comparison; one person can contribute more than one. A percentage among compared cases cannot describe everyone originally offered testing, and an analysis exclusion is not automatically a failed culture. Keep the drug, cancer, treatment history, outcome, clock and assay version attached rather than ranking different studies as competing accuracy scores.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Keep what changed, the comparator, concentration or dose range, timing, assignment, readout and units, sample identities, replicate structure and variability. Repeated wells address variation under their preparation and allocation; independently obtained biological samples address another source of variation. Many wells from one tumour do not become independent patients, and repetition or a small p-value does not repair a missing comparison. A two-drug experiment needs vehicle, both single drugs and the combination. A larger combination effect than either single drug is not automatically synergy; that claim needs a stated reference model.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The prospective single-arm SENSOR study enrolled 61 people with metastatic colorectal cancer: 54 were eligible, 31 organoids were generated, 25 cultures were screened against eight drugs and nineteen showed a substantial laboratory response. Six people received an organoid-selected treatment, three vistusertib and three capivasertib, with no objective clinical responses. That observation concerns this panel and selected population; it neither establishes benefit from using the assay nor proves that every organoid method is ineffective. Guillen and colleagues' breast-model report describes a complete response in one person with metastatic triple-negative disease after a model-nominated treatment. That case demonstrates feasibility, without a comparison estimating how often the strategy helps.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Randomised outcome evidence must be assessed for the named assay and use rather than declared absent for all functional testing in solid tumours. Ranjan and colleagues reported a 2023 trial of ChemoID selection versus physician choice from the same chemotherapy list in 78 people with recurrent glioblastoma under the 2016 WHO definition. Enrolment stopped after a prespecified efficacy analysis; the intention-to-treat report gave median overall survival of twelve versus 7.5 months. Participants could provide viable tumour through surgery or biopsy, so the findings do not include every patient with recurrent glioblastoma. Cordgenics supported the assay resources, and two authors declared licensed intellectual-property interests. This is evidence for the studied strategy and population, without validating another assay, organoid system, postoperative breast decision or universal treatment rule.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Conventional xenografts, epithelial organoids and short-term fragments make different trade-offs. Xenografts add a living host with mouse support and exposure. Organoids expand selected populations in supplied culture conditions. Fragments can retain local neighbours briefly without perfused circulation. This comparison describes preparations and decision windows; the existing model-context framework owns the broader question of intended-use validation.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Organoids self-organise selected structural or functional tissue features in three-dimensional culture. Patient-derived tumour organoids are one member of this broader family, rather than complete copies of a patient. Establishment and growth conditions select cells, and identity and relevant properties need checking against the source specimen. Conventional epithelial cultures often omit immune and supporting populations; specialised retention or added co-cultures require method-specific evidence. Their use for mechanism and drug-response experiments does not by itself establish clinical utility.

Dijkstra and colleagues combined autologous blood lymphocytes with tumour organoids from mismatch repair-deficient colorectal cancer and from non-small-cell lung cancer, with enrichment and later killing measurements as separate stages. Presence, activation, tumour recognition and killing require different observations; neither model label establishes universal patient prediction.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. coverageEvidence.excerpt: The prospective single-arm SENSOR study enrolled 61 people with metastatic colorectal cancer: 54 were eligible, 31 organoids were generated, 25 cultures were screened against eight drugs and nineteen showed a substantial laboratory response. Six people received an organoid-selected treatment, three vistusertib and three capivasertib, with no objective clinical responses. That observation concerns this panel and selected population; it neither establishes benefit from using the assay nor proves that every organoid method is ineffective. Guillen and colleagues' breast-model report describes a complete response in one person with metastatic triple-negative disease after a model-nominated treatment. That case demonstrates feasibility, without a comparison estimating how often the strategy helps.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Randomised outcome evidence must be assessed for the named assay and use rather than declared absent for all functional testing in solid tumours. Ranjan and colleagues reported a 2023 trial of ChemoID selection versus physician choice from the same chemotherapy list in 78 people with recurrent glioblastoma under the 2016 WHO definition. Enrolment stopped after a prespecified efficacy analysis; the intention-to-treat report gave median overall survival of twelve versus 7.5 months. Participants could provide viable tumour through surgery or biopsy, so the findings do not include every patient with recurrent glioblastoma. Cordgenics supported the assay resources, and two authors declared licensed intellectual-property interests. This is evidence for the studied strategy and population, without validating another assay, organoid system, postoperative breast decision or universal treatment rule.

points.requirement: **A controlled model response tests a mechanism within the model's scope; translation to patients is the next evidence question.**

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A controlled perturbation deliberately changes a defined factor and measures the response against appropriate comparison conditions. Vehicle, positive, negative and mechanism controls answer different questions. A reproducible response can support an experimental claim without establishing its proposed mechanism or patient benefit. Baseline growth, timing, dose and the actual unit assigned to treatment matter.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:controlled-perturbation: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: **[Multi-omic integration](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/computational-analysis/multi-omic-integration) is a careful argument: name the claim, connect compatible observations, and state the gap before any clinical conclusion.**

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Integration card for combining molecular layers (a reading guide, not a score). Measures: relationships among named layers, not one universal multi-omic score. How: match evidence records, check quality and comparability, harmonise features, compare or model, then evaluate the stated question. Input and tissue cost: existing assay data and metadata; computation uses no extra tissue, but each original assay has its own specimen cost. Output and units: a comparison, factors, clusters or predictions, with the model version and underlying units. Thresholds: specific to the method and validated task, and none applies to every integration. Failure modes: sample swaps, cell-mixture changes, batch confounding, missing data and information leaking into evaluation. Cannot establish alone: causation, malignant-cell target location or better treatment outcomes. Validation tier: research integration gives neither its inputs nor its resulting model a clinical status.

A separate RNA assay showing a splice junction is a new measurement that answers a new question, and it does not by itself confirm the DNA call.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: **Before you start:** [The evidence chain from variant to benefit](/wiki/education/concepts/evidence-and-statistics/reasoning-tools/evidence-chain-variant-to-benefit) lays out the bridges. [Genomic scars](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/genome-instability-and-repair/genomic-scars) record past repair failure. [Actionability](/wiki/education/concepts/evidence-and-statistics/biomarkers/actionability) separates a plausible target from an evidence-supported option. [Germline versus somatic](/wiki/education/concepts/biology-basics/genetics/germline-vs-somatic) preserves origin. [Prognostic versus predictive](/wiki/education/concepts/evidence-and-statistics/biomarkers/prognostic-vs-predictive) separates forecasting from treatment selection.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Biallelic inactivation concerns whether either parental contribution still supplies useful function in the relevant cancer-cell population, rather than simply counting two physical DNA copies or two events somewhere in a tissue. A damaging change plus loss of the other contribution can support it, but phasing, allele-specific copy state, consequence and cell mixture matter. High VAF alone cannot establish this state. Nguyen and colleagues' pan-cancer analysis associated particular biallelic repair-gene alterations with genomic damage patterns; that association does not make every variant in every repair gene functionally equivalent or establish present drug sensitivity.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
RAD51 nuclear foci are assemblies of a protein involved in homologous recombination. Their interpretation depends on the sampled tumour cells, cell-cycle state, damage, staining, scoring and controls. A low count without enough informative cycling cells is uninformative rather than proof that repair is absent. The assay is a functional surrogate, not direct observation of every completed repair event.

Cruz and colleagues in 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived breast cancer models and retrospective tumour specimens. Castroviejo-Bermejo and colleagues separately compared RAD51 and genomic HRD scores against olaparib response in breast cancer xenografts, then assessed feasibility in archival breast samples, including PALB2-related cancers. The latter clinical samples established feasibility, rather than a randomised benefit from choosing treatment with the assay.

A scar records accumulated genomic changes; a suitably controlled RAD51 result asks about a present repair-related state. Repair-restoring changes and acquired foci were observed in selected resistant BRCA-mutated breast cancers, but those small cohorts do not establish a universal treatment-switch rule. Use the actual assay version, informative-cell requirements and intended-use validation. A research score cannot replace the biomarker, disease and companion-test conditions of a medicine's label.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:rad51-foci-assay: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Specimen and assay card. Record donor/site/time, living preparation, transport and processing, initial composition, culture history, assay version, concentrations, exposure duration, replicates and control range. Fixed tissue cannot supply living cells; whether previously frozen material can supply the required viable preparation must be demonstrated for that protocol. Input suitability and recovery must be demonstrated for the method. Testing and endpoint processing use finite material. Output needs units, denominator, normalisation and uncertainty; acceptance criteria must be defined for the actual method. Name whether the preparation is dissociated cells, a fresh fragment or an expanded organoid. Mixed samples include normal neighbours, and expansion can change the represented populations.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: This is more useful than “multi-omics found a repair problem.” Another reader can inspect each row and see where confidence changed.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: [Homologous recombination (HR)](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/genome-instability-and-repair/homologous-recombination-and-hrd) repairs certain double-strand DNA breaks using a matching template; homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) means that repair is impaired. When it fails for a long time, the genome accumulates a characteristic pattern of damage, a **genomic scar**. Scar methods summarize different features: loss of heterozygosity (LOH), telomeric allelic imbalance (TAI) and large-scale state transitions (LST), and their cutoffs are method-specific. [Mutational signatures](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/genome-instability-and-repair/mutational-signatures) are another kind of pattern.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A composite score compresses selected features of a tumour's chromosome history. Like a summary of past events, it leaves details out; like numbers on differently calibrated scales, the same numerical value need not have the same meaning in two laboratories. The composite count is not a percentage of repair-deficient cells. Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity can replace two parental versions with copies of one version without reducing the total copy number, so loss of heterozygosity is not always loss of a physical chromosome copy.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The specimen and analysis are part of the result. Telli used tumour DNA, a genome-wide SNP panel, allele-imbalance profiles and prespecified counting rules; if the score failed and BRCA testing was negative or failed, HRD status was undetermined. A failed result is not a low score. Reports should identify the assay version, usable tumour content, DNA input/quality, copy-number and allele-balance method, segmentation, and purity/ploidy assumptions. HRDetect was explored in a small biopsy series and one formalin-fixed specimen with substantial sequencing artefact; those demonstrations do not certify every degraded specimen. RAD51 foci ask a different, conditional question about present repair. A BRCA reversion or 53BP1 loss is not itself a measured new scar score or proof of restored function.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
RAD51 nuclear foci are assemblies of a protein involved in homologous recombination. Their interpretation depends on the sampled tumour cells, cell-cycle state, damage, staining, scoring and controls. A low count without enough informative cycling cells is uninformative rather than proof that repair is absent. The assay is a functional surrogate, not direct observation of every completed repair event.

Cruz and colleagues in 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived breast cancer models and retrospective tumour specimens. Castroviejo-Bermejo and colleagues separately compared RAD51 and genomic HRD scores against olaparib response in breast cancer xenografts, then assessed feasibility in archival breast samples, including PALB2-related cancers. The latter clinical samples established feasibility, rather than a randomised benefit from choosing treatment with the assay.

A scar records accumulated genomic changes; a suitably controlled RAD51 result asks about a present repair-related state. Repair-restoring changes and acquired foci were observed in selected resistant BRCA-mutated breast cancers, but those small cohorts do not establish a universal treatment-switch rule. Use the actual assay version, informative-cell requirements and intended-use validation. A research score cannot replace the biomarker, disease and companion-test conditions of a medicine's label.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Even a persuasive biological chain needs treatment evidence in the disease, setting, comparator, outcome and eligibility that apply. A real example shows the gate. The OlympiA trial randomized 1,836 people with high-risk HER2-negative early breast cancer and a **germline** BRCA1 or BRCA2 variant to a year of olaparib or placebo after standard treatment. Three-year invasive disease-free survival was 85.9% versus 77.1% (hazard ratio 0.58) ([Tutt et al., 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34081848/)). The approved adjuvant use follows that population, with a validated germline test.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: OlympiA, trial NCT02032823 sponsored by AstraZeneca, NRG Oncology and the Breast International Group and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, showed that a year of the PARP inhibitor olaparib after standard treatment improves survival in women with germline BRCA mutations and high-risk, HER2-negative early breast cancer, about eighty percent of whom had triple-negative disease. It randomised 1,836 patients to olaparib or placebo, met its primary invasive disease-free survival endpoint and showed an overall survival benefit that was sustained at six years. It makes germline testing a treatment decision for every such patient, and whether the benefit extends to somatic or non-BRCA HRD alterations is the open question.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The U.S. olaparib label effective July 2025 permits olaparib plus bevacizumab maintenance for adults with HRD-positive advanced epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer in complete or partial response to first-line platinum; the specified HRD definition includes a deleterious or suspected-deleterious BRCA alteration and/or genomic instability, with an approved companion test. Its early-breast indication instead requires a deleterious or suspected-deleterious germline BRCA alteration, HER2-negative high-risk disease and prior neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy, with the approved test. A tumour-only BRCA finding or an arbitrary high scar number does not substitute for these conditions.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. Eligibility exclusions, absent tumour, laboratory failures, missing outcomes and people not receiving the treatment belong to different steps. State whether the unit is a person, specimen or treatment comparison; one person can contribute more than one. A percentage among compared cases cannot describe everyone originally offered testing, and an analysis exclusion is not automatically a failed culture. Keep the drug, cancer, treatment history, outcome, clock and assay version attached rather than ranking different studies as competing accuracy scores.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The category concerns a device and a corresponding treatment use. FDA describes roles involving likely benefit, serious-adverse-effect risk or specified treatment monitoring. Check both the treatment and diagnostic labeling, including specimen, disease, biomarker and decision rule. A molecular report listing a drug is not by itself a companion-diagnostic authorization. Similar gene names do not establish assay interchangeability, and a positive result does not promise a response.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Three examples separate intended uses. Validated ER immunohistochemistry in invasive breast cancer, with appropriate tissue handling, tumour-nucleus scoring and controls, has a marker-specific pathology and endocrine-treatment assessment role; it does not validate a new RNA score as a substitute. In a wholly fictional second example, assay T version 1 detects alteration M in fixed tumour tissue under rule R, and Drug A requires exactly that result in setting S. The stipulated match supplies that requirement within the exercise, without promising benefit; another specimen, result type or setting needs evidence for the changed use. A third fictional score Q combines RNA, spatial neighbourhoods and a derived culture response to propose Drug A. Reproducibility and biological support can justify research, but do not establish that Q-guided care improves outcomes against an appropriate comparator. A laboratory certificate does not supply that missing evidence. Useful research and an established clinical use can appear on different parts of one report.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Start with the intended decision, not the technology's name. A [companion diagnostic](/wiki/education/concepts/access-and-regulation/approval/companion-diagnostics) supplies treatment-linked information for a specified use. [Research use only, laboratory-developed test, CLIA certification and FDA authorization](/wiki/education/concepts/access-and-regulation/approval/ruo-ldt-clia-and-fda-authorization) describe different things: a product's purpose, where a test was developed, laboratory standards under the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments, and Food and Drug Administration review of a product for an intended use. None is a universal evidence score.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The category concerns a device and a corresponding treatment use. FDA describes roles involving likely benefit, serious-adverse-effect risk or specified treatment monitoring. Check both the treatment and diagnostic labeling, including specimen, disease, biomarker and decision rule. A molecular report listing a drug is not by itself a companion-diagnostic authorization. Similar gene names do not establish assay interchangeability, and a positive result does not promise a response.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: **A. Validated, marker-specific pathology use.** Establish estrogen receptor (ER) status in invasive breast cancer by validated [immunohistochemistry](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/pathology-readouts/immunohistochemistry) on properly fixed tissue with controls. The 2020 guideline from the American Society of Clinical Oncology and College of American Pathologists keeps an ER-low-positive category, and an uninterpretable result is not negative ([guideline](https://www.cap.org/cap-guidelines/estrogen-and-progesterone-receptor-testing-in-breast-cancer-guideline-update/)). This does not validate a new RNA score as a substitute.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The oestrogen receptor is an intracellular protein involved in responses to oestrogen and regulation of gene expression. A clinical ER result measures receptor staining in identified tumour-cell nuclei, not the amount of oestrogen in blood or every downstream signal.

The ASCO/CAP invasive-breast guideline uses validated immunohistochemistry: at least 1% stained tumour-cell nuclei is positive, below 1% is negative, and 1% to 10% is reported as ER-low positive. These cancers are heterogeneous and can have features resembling ER-negative disease, but they remain ER-positive. Limited evidence suggests possible endocrine benefit, so the category supports consideration of endocrine treatment rather than a guaranteed response or a treatment mandate.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The measurement route is tissue, identification of invasive tumour cells, a validated nuclear stain, review of controls, percentage and intensity, then interpretation. Keep the specimen/block and collection context; IHC uses tissue sections. Percentage counts positive nuclei among the intended tumour cells, while intensity describes stain strength. Poor preservation, artefact or failed controls can prevent interpretation: uninterpretable does not mean negative. A bulk RNA result does not replace validated clinical IHC. ASCO/CAP recommends ER testing in DCIS to assess potential endocrine risk reduction, with PR optional there; invasive and in-situ contexts should be stated.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: For a fictional invasive tumour with adequate controls, ER staining in 4% of tumour-cell nuclei is ER-low positive. Preserve the stain denominator, intensity and category alongside that separate expression result. If controls fail, resolve the testing problem before assigning a negative category. ER and PR results remain separate observations.

points.heading: Ask whether the observations are independent
points.requirement: Carry every factual, numeric, causal and interpretive clause, or an explicit supported correction. Exact field containment alone cannot establish semantic acceptance.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: DNA, RNA and protein inspect different objects, so together they can strengthen a chain. They can also share contamination, wrong cell assignments or the same assumed variant list, so count them as [lesson 8](/wiki/education/guides/what-multi-omics-tells-us/08-choose-the-comparison#count-independent-observations-not-reports) does: by independent measurement, not by report. For a computed integration, record the model version, missing inputs and which values were filled in by the model.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.
coverageEvidence.sourceScope: prior:multi-omic-integration: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Integration card for combining molecular layers (a reading guide, not a score). Measures: relationships among named layers, not one universal multi-omic score. How: match evidence records, check quality and comparability, harmonise features, compare or model, then evaluate the stated question. Input and tissue cost: existing assay data and metadata; computation uses no extra tissue, but each original assay has its own specimen cost. Output and units: a comparison, factors, clusters or predictions, with the model version and underlying units. Thresholds: specific to the method and validated task, and none applies to every integration. Failure modes: sample swaps, cell-mixture changes, batch confounding, missing data and information leaking into evaluation. Cannot establish alone: causation, malignant-cell target location or better treatment outcomes. Validation tier: research integration gives neither its inputs nor its resulting model a clinical status.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Figure reading (fictional): the same DNA call, a T in the sequence A C T G A, is copied into Report A, Report B and Report C, which is one observation reported three times. A separate RNA assay showing a splice junction is a new measurement that answers a new question, and it does not by itself confirm the DNA call.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: - Treating a scar as current function, or activity as dependence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A composite score compresses selected features of a tumour's chromosome history. Like a summary of past events, it leaves details out; like numbers on differently calibrated scales, the same numerical value need not have the same meaning in two laboratories. The composite count is not a percentage of repair-deficient cells. Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity can replace two parental versions with copies of one version without reducing the total copy number, so loss of heterozygosity is not always loss of a physical chromosome copy.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The specimen and analysis are part of the result. A failed result is not a low score. Reports should identify the assay version, usable tumour content, DNA input/quality, copy-number and allele-balance method, segmentation, and purity/ploidy assumptions. HRDetect was explored in a small biopsy series and one formalin-fixed specimen with substantial sequencing artefact; those demonstrations do not certify every degraded specimen. RAD51 foci ask a different, conditional question about present repair. A BRCA reversion or 53BP1 loss is not itself a measured new scar score or proof of restored function.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
RAD51 nuclear foci are assemblies of a protein involved in homologous recombination. Their interpretation depends on the sampled tumour cells, cell-cycle state, damage, staining, scoring and controls. A low count without enough informative cycling cells is uninformative rather than proof that repair is absent. The assay is a functional surrogate, not direct observation of every completed repair event.

Cruz and colleagues in 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived breast cancer models and retrospective tumour specimens. Castroviejo-Bermejo and colleagues separately compared RAD51 and genomic HRD scores against olaparib response in breast cancer xenografts, then assessed feasibility in archival breast samples, including PALB2-related cancers. The latter clinical samples established feasibility, rather than a randomised benefit from choosing treatment with the assay.

A scar records accumulated genomic changes; a suitably controlled RAD51 result asks about a present repair-related state. Repair-restoring changes and acquired foci were observed in selected resistant BRCA-mutated breast cancers, but those small cohorts do not establish a universal treatment-switch rule. Use the actual assay version, informative-cell requirements and intended-use validation. A research score cannot replace the biomarker, disease and companion-test conditions of a medicine's label.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. coverageEvidence.excerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: A practical report reading starts with six questions: what specimen, region, date and treatment context were sampled; what object and units were measured with which assay version; whether the result is signed clinical, preliminary, research or model-predicted evidence; which controls or reference support the comparison; what remains unmeasured; and which actual decision could change. Molecular layer and resolution are separate axes. Mapping 500 RNA targets in one section adds location relative to a pooled RNA result, while the measured layer remains RNA. coverageEvidence.excerpt: Integration card for combining molecular layers (a reading guide, not a score). Measures: relationships among named layers, not one universal multi-omic score. How: match evidence records, check quality and comparability, harmonise features, compare or model, then evaluate the stated question. Output and units: a comparison, factors, clusters or predictions, with the model version and underlying units. Thresholds: specific to the method and validated task, and none applies to every integration. Failure modes: sample swaps, cell-mixture changes, batch confounding, missing data and information leaking into evaluation. Cannot establish alone: causation, malignant-cell target location or better treatment outcomes. Validation tier: research integration gives neither its inputs nor its resulting model a clinical status.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In a fictional comparison, gene R is high in cancer cells, low in fibroblasts and similarly high in normal luminal epithelial cells. The first contrast supports higher expression than fibroblasts, even if it passes a statistical threshold; it does not establish cancer selectivity. The normal epithelial comparison addresses that claim more closely, while leaving other organs, cell states and target accessibility untested. If that reference group is tiny, contaminated or prepared differently, preserve the unresolved comparison rather than declaring selectivity or exact equality. Normal epithelial cells can also contribute familiar lineage markers to a tumour specimen. An image-based tumour mask is an assignment that needs validation for its actual method and specimens, rather than automatic proof that every included cell is malignant.
